title.zh: 第六 禮儀下 大喪諸侯王列侯始封貴人公主薨
title.raw: 第六 禮儀下 大喪諸侯王列侯始封貴人公主薨 Volume 96: Etiquette Part Three

sentences.zh: 後漢書志第六 禮儀下 大喪諸侯王列侯始封貴人公主薨 不豫，太醫令丞將醫人，就進所宜藥。

translations.literal: Book of Later Han, Treatise 6 — "Ritual and Etiquette, Part Two: Major Mourning — When a feudatory king, full marquis, first-enfeoffed noble, exalted lady, or princess dies." When the patient is indisposed, the Grand Physician and his Assistant lead physicians forward to administer suitable medicines.
translations.idiomatic: *Hou Hanshu*, Treatise 6, "Ritual and Etiquette, Part Two: State Funerals for Feudatory Kings, Full Marquises, Newly Enfeoffed Nobles, Exalted Ladies, and Princesses." While the patient remains unwell, the Grand Physician and his Assistant bring physicians to the bedside to prescribe and administer appropriate drugs.

sentences.zh: 嘗藥監、近臣中常侍、小黃門皆先嘗藥，過量十二。

translations.literal: The drug-tasting supervisor, favored attendants among the chief eunuchs, and junior Yellow Gates all taste the medicine first, exceeding the measured dose by twelve parts.
translations.idiomatic: The supervisor of drug sampling, together with intimate attendants—the chief eunuchs and junior Yellow Gates—samples the draught before it is given, deliberately drawing off more than the nominal dose as a safeguard.

sentences.zh: 公卿朝臣問起居無閒。

translations.literal: The three dukes and court officials inquire after daily welfare without interval.
translations.idiomatic: Grandees and courtiers attend constantly, asking after the patient’s condition without pause.

sentences.zh: 太尉告請南郊，司徒、司空告請宗廟，告五獄、四瀆、腢祀，並禱求福。

translations.literal: The Grand Commandant announces and petitions at the Southern Suburban Altar; the Minister of Education and the Minister of Works announce and petition at the ancestral temples; they report to the Five Marchmounts, the Four Great Rivers, and collective sacrifices, and together pray for blessing.
translations.idiomatic: The Grand Commandant petitions Heaven at the southern suburban altar; the Ministers of Education and of Works petition the imperial temples; announcements go out to the Five Marchmounts and Four Great Rivers, to mass offerings, and supplications are made in concert for divine favor.

sentences.zh: 疾病，公卿復如禮。

translations.literal: If there is illness, the three dukes again act according to the rites.
translations.idiomatic: Should the illness continue, the three dukes repeat the observances prescribed by ritual.

sentences.zh: 注[一]漢舊儀曰：「帝崩，唅以珠，纏以緹繒十二重。

translations.literal: Comment [1] *Han ji yi* says: "When the emperor died, a pearl was placed in the mouth; he was wrapped in twelve layers of orange-red silk.
translations.idiomatic: Note [1] — the *Han Court Ceremonial* records: “At the emperor’s death, a pearl was placed in the mouth, and the body was wound in twelve layers of fine orange-red silk.”

sentences.zh: 以玉為襦，如鎧狀，連縫之，以黃金為縷。

translations.literal: Jade was fashioned into a short upper garment like armour, stitched in one piece, with yellow gold for the thread.
translations.idiomatic: A jade upper garment shaped like lamellar armour was sewn in one continuous piece, the seams worked with gold thread.

sentences.zh: 腰以下以玉為札，長一尺，*[廣]*二寸半，為柙，下至足，亦縫以黃金鏤。

translations.literal: Below the waist jade plaques were used, one foot long, *[wide]* two and a half inches, forming a casing down to the feet, also stitched with openwork gold.
translations.idiomatic: From the waist down, jade tablets a foot long and two and a half inches wide formed a sheath to the feet, likewise sewn with pierced gold ornament.

translations.literal: A lone asterisk marks lacunae or editorial uncertainty in the received text.
translations.idiomatic: The apparatus marks this point with a lone asterisk, signaling missing or uncertain text in the transmission.

translations.literal: A marginal gloss reads qing 請.
translations.idiomatic: A manuscript gloss inserts the character qing 請 at this break in the quotation.

sentences.zh: *諸衣衿斂之。

translations.literal: *All garments for collars are gathered for laying-in.
translations.idiomatic: Every collar-piece and garment used in the enshrouding is assembled for the laying-in.

sentences.zh: 凡乘輿衣服，已御，輒藏之，崩皆以斂。」

translations.literal: All imperial garments, once worn, are stored away; at death they are all used for enshrouding."
translations.idiomatic: Whatever riding or court dress the sovereign had already worn was archived; at death those very fabrics were brought out to shroud the body.”

sentences.zh: 注[二]禮稽命征曰：「天子飯以珠，唅以玉。

translations.literal: Comment [2] *Li ji ming zheng* says: "The Son of Heaven is fed pearl and receives jade in the mouth.
translations.idiomatic: Note [2] — *Rites: Auspicious Mandate* states: “The Son of Heaven is fed grain mixed with pearl and holds a jade tablet in the mouth.”

sentences.zh: 諸侯飯以珠，唅以*

translations.literal: Feudatories are fed pearl and receive in the mouth *
translations.idiomatic: Feudal lords are fed pearl and hold in the mouth—

translations.literal: A marginal gloss reads zhu 珠 (pearl).
translations.idiomatic: The apparatus supplies zhu 珠, indicating “pearl” belongs in the lacuna.

translations.literal: **[jade disk]*."
translations.idiomatic: —a *bi* disk of jade.”

sentences.zh: 卿大夫、士飯以珠，唅以貝。」

translations.literal: Grand ministers, great officers, and gentlemen are fed pearl and receive shell in the mouth."
translations.idiomatic: Ministers, grand officers, and common gentlemen are fed pearl and hold a cowrie in the mouth.”

sentences.zh: 注[三]周禮：「凌人，天子喪，供夷盤冰。

translations.literal: Comment [3] *Zhou li*: "The ice officer, at the Son of Heaven’s funeral, supplies the broad ice-trays with ice.
translations.idiomatic: Note [3] — *Rites of Zhou*: “The Keeper of Ice, when the Son of Heaven dies, supplies the broad basins with ice.”

sentences.zh: 」鄭玄曰：「夷之言屍也，實冰於盤中，置之屍默之下，所以寒屍也。

translations.literal: " Zheng Xuan says: "‘Yi’ means ‘corpse’; ice is packed in the tray and placed beneath the silent corpse, thereby to chill the body.
translations.idiomatic: Zheng Xuan explains: “*Yi* here means the corpse; ice is piled in the basin and set under the bier to cool the remains.”

sentences.zh: 」漢禮器制度：「大盤廣八尺，長一丈二尺，深三尺，漆赤中。」

translations.literal: " *Han li qi zhi du*: "The great tray is eight feet wide, twelve feet long, and three feet deep, lacquered red inside."
translations.idiomatic: The *Han Ritual Vessel Regulations* add: “The great basin measures eight feet across, twelve feet long, and three feet deep, lacquered vermilion within.”

sentences.zh: 注[四]應劭曰：「凡與郡國守相竹使符，皆以竹箭五枚，長五寸，鐫刻篆書第一至第五。

translations.literal: Comment [4] Ying Shao says: "Whenever bamboo tallies are issued to commandery and kingdom shepherds and chancellors, they are all of bamboo arrow five pieces, five inches long, engraved in seal script with numbers one through fifth.
translations.idiomatic: Note [4] — Ying Shao: “Whenever bamboo dispatch tallies are given to shepherds and chancellors of commanderies and kingdoms, five slips of arrow bamboo, each five inches long, are cut and engraved in seal script with the numerals first through fifth.”

sentences.zh: 」張晏曰：「符以代古之珪璋，從簡易也。

translations.literal: " Zhang Yan says: "The tallies replace the ancient *gui* and *zhang* tablets, following simplicity.
translations.idiomatic: Zhang Yan adds: “Tallies stand in for the old jade *gui* and *zhang*, for ease of use.”

sentences.zh: 」此下大喪符，亦猶斯比。

translations.literal: " The great-mourning tallies below are likewise of this sort.
translations.idiomatic: The funeral tallies described below follow the same pattern.

sentences.zh: 注[五]漢舊制，發兵皆以銅虎符，其餘徵調，竹使而已。

translations.literal: Comment [5] Han old system: raising troops always used bronze tiger tallies; other levies used bamboo dispatch tallies only.
translations.idiomatic: Note [5] — Under Han precedent, mobilization required matched bronze tiger tallies; ordinary requisitions relied on bamboo tallies alone.

sentences.zh: 符第合會為大信，見杜詩傳。

translations.literal: The tallies’ serial numbers must join to constitute great trust; see Du’s commentary.
translations.idiomatic: When the halves of a tally mate, that constitutes the supreme proof of authenticity, as Du’s tradition explains.

sentences.zh: 注[六]周禮：「駔珪、璋、璧、琮、琥、璜之渠眉，疏璧、琮以斂屍。

translations.literal: Comment [6] *Zhou li*: "Decorate the channels and brow-ridges of *gui*, *zhang*, *bi*, *cong*, *hu*, and *huang*; pierce *bi* and *cong* to lay on the corpse.
translations.idiomatic: Note [6] — *Rites of Zhou*: “Channel the outer ridges of *gui*, *zhang*, *bi*, *cong*, *hu*, and *huang*; bore through *bi* and *cong* to secure them on the corpse.”

sentences.zh: 」鄭司農曰：「駔，外有捷盧也。

translations.literal: " Director Zheng says: "‘Decorate’ means there is an outer flange.
translations.idiomatic: Director Zheng (Zheng Zhong) says: “‘Decorate’ means an outer raised rim.”

sentences.zh: 謂珪、璋、璧、琮、琥、璜皆為開渠，為眉瑑，沙除以斂屍，令汁得流去也。

translations.literal: " It means *gui*, *zhang*, *bi*, *cong*, *hu*, and *huang* all have open channels carved as brow-lines, sanded smooth to lay on the corpse so effusion may drain away.
translations.idiomatic: He means every type of jade—*gui*, *zhang*, *bi*, *cong*, *hu*, and *huang*—is grooved and ridged, the channels smoothed, so fluid can run off when the pieces lie on the body.

sentences.zh: 」鄭玄曰：「以斂屍者，以大斂焉加之也。

translations.literal: " Zheng Xuan says: "Those used to lay on the corpse are placed at the great laying-in.
translations.idiomatic: Zheng Xuan clarifies: “Those that cover the corpse are added at the great enshrouding.”

sentences.zh: 渠眉，玉飾之溝瑑也，以組穿聯六玉溝瑑之中以斂屍。

translations.literal: The channel-brow is a grooved ridge ornament on the jade; cords are threaded through the six jades’ grooves to bind them on the corpse.
translations.idiomatic: The “channel-brow” is the carved gutter along each piece; silk cords lace the six jades through those grooves to fix them to the remains.

sentences.zh: 珪在左，璋在首，琥在右，璜在足，璧在背，琮在腹，蓋取象方明神之也。

translations.literal: The *gui* is at the left, the *zhang* at the head, the *hu* at the right, the *huang* at the feet, the *bi* at the back, and the *cong* at the belly, thereby imaging the square bright spirit.
translations.idiomatic: The *gui* goes to the left, the *zhang* at the crown, the *hu* to the right, the *huang* at the feet, the *bi* behind the back, and the *cong* over the belly—an arrangement that mirrors the spirit tablet’s four sides.

sentences.zh: 疏璧、琮者，通於天地。」

translations.literal: " Pierced *bi* and *cong* mean communication with Heaven and Earth."
translations.idiomatic: “Pierced *bi* and *cong*” signify passage between Heaven and Earth.”

sentences.zh: 注[七]喪大記曰：「君蓋用漆，三衽三束。

translations.literal: Comment [7] *Sang da ji* says: "The lord’s cover is lacquered, with three waist-bands and three bindings.
translations.idiomatic: Note [7] — *Record of Mourning Rites*: “The ruler’s lid is lacquered, with three waist-wrappings and three lashings.”

sentences.zh: 」鄭玄注曰：「衽，小腰。」

translations.literal: " Zheng Xuan’s commentary says: "The waist-band is the small girdle."
translations.idiomatic: Zheng Xuan glosses: “The *ren* is the narrow waist sash.”

sentences.zh: 三公奏尚書顧命，太子即日即天子位於柩前，請太子即皇帝位，皇后為皇太后。

translations.literal: The three dukes memorialize the *Shang shu* “Charge at the Border,” and the heir apparent that same day takes the Son of Heaven’s position before the bier; they request the heir to assume the imperial seat and the empress to become empress dowager.
translations.idiomatic: The three dukes present the *Canon of Documents* chapter “Testamentary Charge,” and the crown prince the same day mounts the throne before the coffin; memorialists ask him to take the imperial title and the consort to become empress dowager.

sentences.zh: 奏可。

translations.literal: Memorial approved.
translations.idiomatic: The throne endorsed the memorial.

sentences.zh: 腢臣皆出，吉服入會如儀。

translations.literal: All ministers go out, then enter again in auspicious dress according to the observances.
translations.idiomatic: The entire body of officials withdraws, then re-enters in festive court dress as the liturgy prescribes.

sentences.zh: 太尉升自阼階，當柩御坐北面稽首，讀策畢，以傳國玉璽綬東面跪授皇太子，即皇帝位。

translations.literal: The Grand Commandant ascends the eastern steps, stands north-facing before the catafalque and the imperial seat, performs a forehead knock, finishes reading the edict, and kneeling eastward hands the heir the imperial seal-cord; the heir takes the throne.
translations.idiomatic: The Grand Commandant mounts the eastern staircase, faces north before bier and throne, kowtows, reads the accession rescript to the end, then kneels toward the east and delivers the dynastic seal and ribbon to the crown prince, who thereby ascends.

sentences.zh: 中黃門掌兵以玉具、隨侯珠、斬蛇寶□授太尉，告令腢臣，腢臣皆伏稱萬歲。

translations.literal: A chief eunuch in charge of arms presents to the Grand Commandant the jade-hilted sword, the Marquis of Sui pearl, and the sword that slew the serpent [?] treasure □; he is told to inform all ministers, and all ministers prostrate themselves shouting “Ten thousand years!”
translations.idiomatic: Palace eunuchs bearing arms hand the Grand Commandant the jade-mounted blade, the pearl of the Marquis of Sui, and the heirloom sword of Han’s founding—text damaged—then proclaim the order to the assembly, which prostrates itself and acclaims the new reign.

sentences.zh: 或大赦天下。

translations.literal: Perhaps a general amnesty is proclaimed for the realm.
translations.idiomatic: Often a universal pardon follows.

sentences.zh: 遣使者詔開城門、宮門，罷屯□兵。

translations.literal: Envoys are sent with edicts to open city and palace gates and to dismiss garrison □ troops.
translations.idiomatic: Messengers bearing edicts open the capital gates and palace portals and stand down the guard contingents—one character illegible in the source.

sentences.zh: 腢臣百官罷，入成喪服如禮。

translations.literal: All ministers and officials are dismissed; they enter again to assume mourning dress according to the rites.
translations.idiomatic: The court retires, then reassembles in full mourning costume as ritual demands.

sentences.zh: 兵官戎。

translations.literal: Military officers in arms.
translations.idiomatic: Officers of the guard remain under arms.

sentences.zh: [一]三公，太常如禮。

translations.literal: [1] The three dukes and the Minister of Ceremonies act according to the rites.
translations.idiomatic: [1] The three dukes and the Minister of Ceremonies perform their parts of the liturgy.

sentences.zh: 注[一]文帝遺詔：「無布車及兵器。

translations.literal: Comment [1] Emperor Wen’s testamentary edict: "No light chariots or weapons of war."
translations.idiomatic: Note [1] — Emperor Wen’s final edict forbade war chariots and weapon displays at his funeral.

sentences.zh: 」應劭曰：「不施輕車介士。」

translations.literal: " Ying Shao says: "No light chariots or armoured escorts."
translations.idiomatic: Ying Shao explains: “That means no swift chariots or armoured guardsmen.”

sentences.zh: 故事：百官五日一會臨，故吏二千石、刺史、在京都郡國上計掾史皆五日一會。

translations.literal: Precedent: all officials hold a joint wailing audience once every five days; former subordinates at two thousand *shi*, regional inspectors, and capital clerks from commanderies and kingdoms on fiscal duty likewise assemble every five days.
translations.idiomatic: By standing rule the bureaucracy gathers for a formal lament once every five days; ex-officials at two-thousand-*shi* rank, provincial inspectors, and accounting clerks posted to the capital from the commanderies join on the same five-day rhythm.

sentences.zh: 天下吏民發喪臨三日。

translations.literal: All officials and commoners in the realm hold mourning audiences for three days.
translations.idiomatic: Throughout the empire, clerks and commoners attend the public lament for three days.

sentences.zh: [一]先葬二日，皆旦晡臨。

translations.literal: [1] Two days before burial, all attend morning and afternoon wailing.
translations.idiomatic: [1] On each of the two days preceding interment, mourners gather at dawn and at the afternoon meal hour.

sentences.zh: 既葬，釋服，無禁嫁娶、祠祀。

translations.literal: After burial, mourning dress is laid aside; there is no prohibition on marriage or sacrifice.
translations.idiomatic: Once the tomb is closed, people may doff sackcloth; weddings and routine sacrifices are no longer banned.

sentences.zh: [二]佐史以下，布衣冠幘，絰帶無過三寸，臨庭中。

translations.literal: [2] Assistants and clerks downward wear cloth caps and headcloths, with mourning cords no wider than three inches, wailing in the courtyard.
translations.idiomatic: [2] Subordinates at assistant rank and below wear plain caps with mourning bands, the hemp cord kept under three inches wide, and lament in the court.

sentences.zh: [三]武吏布幘大冠。

translations.literal: [3] Martial clerks wear cloth kerchiefs and great caps.
translations.idiomatic: [3] Military scribes wear coarse kerchiefs with the “great cap.”

sentences.zh: 大司農出見錢谷，給六丈布直。

translations.literal: The Minister of Finance produces cash and grain and supplies six *zhang* of cloth value.
translations.idiomatic: The Minister of Finance releases coin and grain and issues an allowance equivalent to six *zhang* of cloth.

sentences.zh: 以葬，大紅十五日，小紅十四日，纖七日，釋服。

translations.literal: For the burial: great *hong* fifteen days, lesser *hong* fourteen days, *xian* seven days, then mourning ends.
translations.idiomatic: The graduated mourning runs fifteen days in heavy *hong*, fourteen in lighter *hong*, seven in the finest *xian* weave, after which garments of grief are put off.

sentences.zh: [四]部刺史、二千石、列侯在國者及關內侯、宗室長吏及因郵奉奏，諸侯王遣大夫一人奉奏，吊臣請驛馬露布，奏可。

translations.literal: [4] Regional inspectors, two-thousand-*shi* officials, full marquises resident in their fiefs, nobles within the passes, imperial clansmen of senior rank, and those who report via the post relay; feudatory kings each send a senior minister with a memorial; mourning officials request post-horses and an exposed bulletin—the memorial is approved.
translations.idiomatic: [4] Inspectors, two-thousand-*shi* officers, marquises in their states, nobles inside the passes, senior imperial kinsmen, and relay riders with memorials, plus one grand secretary from each kingdom, may petition for courier mounts and open-dispatch notices; the throne assents.

sentences.zh: 注[一]文帝遺詔：「其令天下吏民，令到，出臨三日，釋服。」

translations.literal: Comment [1] Emperor Wen’s testamentary edict: "Order all officials and commoners: when the notice arrives, attend the lament three days, then lay aside mourning."
translations.idiomatic: Note [1] — Emperor Wen’s edict commanded everyone, on receipt of the bulletin, to mourn three days only, then resume normal dress.

sentences.zh: 注[二]文帝遺詔文有「飲酒食肉自當給，喪事服臨者皆無踐」。

translations.literal: Comment [2] Emperor Wen’s testamentary text contains the phrase "drinking wine and eating meat as supply shall allow; those attending the funeral shall not go barefoot."
translations.idiomatic: Note [2] — The same edict allowed mourners to “drink wine and eat meat as their strength required” and forbade barefoot observance at the lying-in-state.

sentences.zh: 踐，徒跣也。

translations.literal: " *Jian* means walking barefoot.
translations.idiomatic: The gloss explains that *jian* means going unshod.

sentences.zh: 注[三]文帝遺詔：「殿中當臨者，以旦夕各十五舉音，禮畢罷。

translations.literal: Comment [3] Emperor Wen’s edict: "Those who must lament within the palace shall sound fifteen cries at dawn and dusk each, then cease when the rite ends.
translations.idiomatic: Note [3] — Palace mourners were to utter fifteen cries at morning and evening audiences, then stop when the service concluded.

sentences.zh: 非旦夕臨時，禁無得擅哭臨。」

translations.literal: " At other than dawn and dusk audiences, weeping visits are forbidden without authorization."
translations.idiomatic: Outside those set hours, no one might freely enter to weep.”

sentences.zh: 注[四]應劭曰：「紅者，*

translations.literal: Comment [4] Ying Shao says: "‘Hong’ means *
translations.idiomatic: Note [4] — Ying Shao: “*Hong* refers to—

translations.literal: A marginal gloss reads zhong 中 (middle).
translations.idiomatic: The critical note reads zhong 中 (“middle”), guiding how the lacuna should be filled.

sentences.zh: **[小]*祥、大祥以紅為領緣*[也]*。

translations.literal: **[small]* auspicious and great auspicious rites use *hong* for collar borders *[also]*.
translations.idiomatic: —the collar facings dyed *hong* for the lesser and greater auspicious anniversaries of mourning.”

sentences.zh: 纖*[者]*，禫也。

translations.literal: " *Xian* *[means]* the *chan* libation.
translations.idiomatic: *Xian* denotes the final *chan* observance.

sentences.zh: 凡三十六日而釋*[服]*。」

translations.literal: " In all, thirty-six days then mourning is laid aside *[dress]*."
translations.idiomatic: Thirty-six days in all, and mourning dress may be removed.”

sentences.zh: 以木為重，高九尺，廣容八歷，裡以葦席。

translations.literal: A wooden *chong* frame is made, nine feet high, eight *li* wide inside, lined with reed matting.
translations.idiomatic: A wooden outer coffin-frame nine feet tall and eight *li* across—inner measure—is lined with reed screens.

sentences.zh: 巾門、喪帳皆以簟。

translations.literal: The cloth over the gate and mourning curtains are all of bamboo matting.
translations.idiomatic: Door draperies and the mourning pavilion are woven from fine bamboo blinds.

sentences.zh: 車皆去輔轓，疏布惡輪。

translations.literal: All chariots have auxiliary rails and screens removed; wheels are wrapped in coarse cloth.
translations.idiomatic: Every cart in the cortège sheds its side rails and screens; wheels are swathed in open-weave sackcloth.

sentences.zh: 走卒皆布□幘。

translations.literal: Running attendants all wear cloth □ kerchiefs.
translations.idiomatic: Foot-runners wear plain kerchiefs—one character missing in the received text.

sentences.zh: 太僕*[駕]*四輪輈為賓車，大練為屋幙。

translations.literal: The Minister of Transport *[drives]* a four-wheeled hearse shaft as guest chariot, with heavy white silk for the canopy curtain.
translations.idiomatic: The Minister of Transport yokes a four-wheeled bier-wagon draped in heavy white silk for the mourning canopy.

sentences.zh: 中黃門、虎賁各二十人執紼。

translations.literal: Twenty chief eunuchs and twenty tiger guards each hold towing cords.
translations.idiomatic: Twenty palace eunuchs and twenty tiger guards take up the drag-ropes.

sentences.zh: 司空擇土造穿。

translations.literal: The Minister of Works selects earth and digs the shaft.
translations.idiomatic: The Minister of Works chooses the site and opens the grave pit.

sentences.zh: 太史卜日。

translations.literal: The Director of Astronomy divines the day.
translations.idiomatic: The imperial astrologers cast lots for the burial date.

sentences.zh: 謁者二人，中謁者僕射、中謁者副將作，油緹帳以覆坑。

translations.literal: Two heralds, the chief herald’s deputy, and assistant heralds from the Directorate of Works spread an oiled-silk awning over the pit.
translations.idiomatic: Two heralds, with the chief herald’s lieutenant and Works deputies, stretch oiled-crimson curtains over the excavation.

sentences.zh: 方石治黃腸題湊便房如禮。

translations.literal: Square stone, yellow-heart oak header-baulks, and side chambers are prepared according to the rites.
translations.idiomatic: Squared stone, “yellow-gut” timber baulks with mortised ends, and side niches are fitted out as canonical burial architecture prescribes.

sentences.zh: [一] 注[一]漢舊儀略載前漢諸帝壽陵曰：「天子即位明年，將作大匠營陵地，用地七頃，方中用地一頃。

translations.literal: [1] Comment [1] *Han ji yi* briefly records Former Han imperial mausolea: "The year after the Son of Heaven mounts the throne, the Director of Works opens the tomb ground, using seven *qing* of land, the square inner pit one *qing*.
translations.idiomatic: [1] Note [1] — *Han Court Ceremonial* summarizes Western Han imperial tombs: “In the year following accession the Director of Works lays out the necropolis on seven *qing*, of which one *qing* is the sealed core.”

sentences.zh: 深十三丈，堂壇高三丈，墳高十二丈。

translations.literal: Thirteen *zhang* deep, the hall platform three *zhang* high, the mound twelve *zhang* high.
translations.idiomatic: The shaft sinks thirteen *zhang*; the ritual hall rises three *zhang*; the tumulus stands twelve *zhang*.

sentences.zh: 武帝墳高二十丈，明中高一丈七尺，四週二丈，內梓棺柏黃腸題湊，以次百官藏畢。

translations.literal: Emperor Wu’s mound was twenty *zhang* high; the illuminated interior was one *zhang* seven feet on the beam, two *zhang* on the four sides; inner coffins of catalpa, yellow-heart header-baulks, and stored goods of every rank were interred in order.
translations.idiomatic: Emperor Wu’s tumulus reached twenty *zhang*; his lit chamber measured one *zhang* seven feet in height and two *zhang* across the span; inside lay the catalpa inner coffin, yellow-heart baulks, and the ranked grave goods of the whole bureaucracy.

sentences.zh: 其設四通羨門，容大車六馬，皆藏之內方，外陟車石。

translations.literal: It is provided with four communicating cross-passages and gates wide enough for a great cart and six horses; all are sealed within the square inner pit, with ascending cart-stone outside.
translations.idiomatic: Four intersecting vaulted passages admit a six-horse hearse; everything is sealed within the inner square, while sloping stone ramps lead outward.

sentences.zh: 外方立，先閉□戶，戶設夜龍、莫邪□、伏弩，設伏火。

translations.literal: The outer square stands; first the □ doors are closed; the doors set night-dragon [devices], *Mo ye* □, hidden crossbows, and buried trip-fires.
translations.idiomatic: The outer shell is closed; trap doors are sealed with “night-dragon” locks, *Mo ye* blades, spring crossbows, and subterranean flame traps—several graphs damaged.

sentences.zh: 已營陵，餘地為西園後陵，餘地為婕妤以下，次賜親屬功臣。

translations.literal: After the mausoleum is built, remaining land becomes the western park and rear tombs; further surplus goes to concubines ranked *jieyu* downward, then in turn to kin and merit officials.
translations.idiomatic: Surrounding plots become the western pleasure park and satellite tombs; what remains is parceled to concubines below *jieyu* rank, then to relatives and meritorious ministers.

sentences.zh: 」漢書音義曰：「題，頭也。

translations.literal: " *Han shu* yin yi says: "‘Ti’ means head.
translations.idiomatic: The *Han shu* sound-meaning gloss explains: “*Ti* is the head.”

sentences.zh: 湊，以頭向內，所以為固也。

translations.literal: " *Cou* means the ends face inward, thereby to make it firm.
translations.idiomatic: “*Cou* means the beam-ends point inward for structural strength.”

sentences.zh: 便房，藏中便坐也。

translations.literal: " Side chambers are convenient sitting spaces within the vault."
translations.idiomatic: “Side chambers” are antechambers for ritual seating inside the tomb.

sentences.zh: 」皇覽曰：「漢家之葬，方中百步，已穿築為方城。

translations.literal: " *Huang lan* says: "Han burials use a hundred paces square in the pit; once dug it is built up as a square citadel.
translations.idiomatic: The *Imperial Survey* adds: “Han imperial tombs cut a hundred-pace square pit and revet it like a walled city.”

sentences.zh: 其中開四門，四通，足放六馬，然後錯渾雜物，扞漆繒綺金寶米谷，及埋車馬虎豹禽獸。

translations.literal: " Within, four gates open on four passages wide enough for six horses; then mixed treasures—lacquer, silk, brocade, gold, gems, grain, and buried chariots, horses, tigers, leopards, and birds and beasts are packed in.
translations.idiomatic: Four gates lead to vaulted corridors that can take a six-horse team; lacquer, damask, brocade, bullion, grain, chariots, horses, and effigy beasts are heaped in promiscuously.

sentences.zh: 發近郡卒徒，置將軍尉候，以後宮貴幸者皆守園陵。

translations.literal: " Conscripts from neighboring commanderies are mobilized; generals, commandants, and wardens are posted; favored harem ladies are all assigned to guard the park tombs.
translations.idiomatic: Labor levies from nearby commanderies man the site under military overseers; favored consorts are charged with perpetual tending of the imperial grove.

sentences.zh: 元帝葬，乃不用車馬禽獸等物。」

translations.literal: " At Emperor Yuan’s burial, chariots, horses, and living creatures were no longer used."
translations.idiomatic: By Emperor Yuan’s time, live animals and equipage were omitted from the deposit.”

sentences.zh: 大駕，太僕御。

translations.literal: The great chariot train: the Minister of Transport acts as charioteer.
translations.idiomatic: In the grand cortège the Minister of Transport personally drives the lead vehicle.

sentences.zh: 方相氏黃金四目，蒙熊皮，玄衣朱裳，執戈揚楯，立乘四馬先驅。

translations.literal: The *fangxiang* officer wears a four-eyed gold mask, bears a bearskin, black upper garment and vermilion lower, grasps spear and shield, and stands in a four-horse chariot as vanguard.
translations.idiomatic: The exorcist *fangxiang*—golden quad eyes, bearskin cloak, black jacket and scarlet skirt—wields halberd and tasseled shield, riding four horses at the head of the line.

sentences.zh: [一]旗之制，長三仞，十有二游，曳地，畫日、月、升龍，書旐曰「天子之柩」。

translations.literal: [1] Banner regulations: three *ren* long, twelve streamers trailing on the ground, painted with sun, moon, and ascending dragon; the pennant inscription reads "The Son of Heaven’s bier."
translations.idiomatic: [1] Mourning banners stretch three *ren*, carry twelve pendant streamers that sweep the earth, and depict sun, moon, and ascending dragon; the streamer legend reads “The Son of Heaven’s catafalque.”

sentences.zh: 謁者二人立乘六馬為次。

translations.literal: Two heralds stand in a six-horse chariot next in order.
translations.idiomatic: Two heralds follow in a standing six-horse car.

sentences.zh: 大駕甘泉鹵簿，金根容車，蘭台法駕。

translations.literal: The great chariot train follows the sweet-spring palace escort regulations: root-wood guest cars and directorate law chariots.
translations.idiomatic: The procession mirrors the sweet-spring hunt escort: golden-root guest coaches and law-chariots from the secretariat directorate.

sentences.zh: 喪服大行載飾如金根車。

translations.literal: Great mourning outer fittings match the golden-root car’s ornament.
translations.idiomatic: The funeral hearse is draped and ornamented like the golden-root state coach.

sentences.zh: 皇帝從送如禮。

translations.literal: The emperor follows the send-off according to the rites.
translations.idiomatic: The reigning emperor attends the cortège as ritual prescribes.

sentences.zh: 太常上啟奠。

translations.literal: The Minister of Ceremonies opens the libation.
translations.idiomatic: The Minister of Ceremonies begins the offering service.

sentences.zh: 夜漏二十刻，太尉冠長冠，衣齋衣，乘高車，詣殿止車門外。

translations.literal: At the twentieth night-mark the Grand Commandant wears the tall cap, fasting robes, mounts a high cart, and goes to the palace’s chariot-halt gate.
translations.idiomatic: When the clepsydra reaches the twentieth night division, the Grand Commandant dons the elongated cap and abstinence gown, rides a tall wagon, and halts at the inner gate reserved for vehicles.

sentences.zh: 使者到，南向立，太尉進伏拜受詔。

translations.literal: When the envoy arrives, standing south-facing, the Grand Commandant advances, prostrates himself, and receives the edict.
translations.idiomatic: The messenger faces south; the Grand Commandant steps forward, kowtows, and takes the sealed order.

sentences.zh: 太尉詣南郊。

translations.literal: The Grand Commandant goes to the southern suburban altar.
translations.idiomatic: He then proceeds to the southern suburban altar.

sentences.zh: 未盡九刻，大鴻臚設九賓隨立，腢臣入位，太尉行禮。

translations.literal: Before nine night-marks have elapsed, the Grand Herald of Guests arrays the nine guests in attendance; all ministers take their stations, and the Grand Commandant performs the rites.
translations.idiomatic: With more than nine marks of the night still to run, the Grand Herald marshals the nine guest-delegations; the full court is in place while the Grand Commandant executes the liturgy.

sentences.zh: 執事皆冠長冠，衣齋衣。

translations.literal: All officiants wear the elongated cap and fasting garments.
translations.idiomatic: Every officer on duty dons the tall mourning cap and the plain abstinence robes.

sentences.zh: 太祝令跪讀謚策，太尉再拜稽首。

translations.literal: The Grand Invocator kneels and reads the posthumous-title document; the Grand Commandant twice bows with a forehead knock.
translations.idiomatic: The Director of Invocations kneels to intone the *shi* scroll, while the Grand Commandant answers with a double prostration.

sentences.zh: 治禮告事畢。

translations.literal: The Masters of Ceremony announce that the business is finished.
translations.idiomatic: The ritual supervisors declare the southern-altar portion of the service complete.

sentences.zh: 太尉奉謚策，還詣殿端門。

translations.literal: The Grand Commandant bears the posthumous-title document and returns to the main hall’s front gate.
translations.idiomatic: Carrying the sealed rescript of the temple name, the Grand Commandant withdraws to the portal of the great audience hall.

sentences.zh: 太常上祖奠，中黃門尚衣奉衣登容根車。

translations.literal: The Minister of Ceremonies presents the “going-forth” libation; chief eunuchs of the wardrobe bring garments and mount the guest hearse.
translations.idiomatic: The Minister of Ceremonies opens the farewell offering; palace wardrobe eunuchs lift the burial silks onto the root-wood guest coach.

sentences.zh: 東園武士載大行，司徒□行道立車前。

translations.literal: Eastern Park guards bear the catafalque of the late sovereign; the Minister of Education □ walks the route and halts the chariot before it.
translations.idiomatic: Guards from the Eastern Workshop shoulder the great bier; the Minister of Education—one character missing in the text—takes station before the hearse.

sentences.zh: 治禮引太尉入就位，大行車西少南，東面奉*[謚]*策，太史令奉哀策立後。

translations.literal: The Masters of Ceremony lead the Grand Commandant to his place; the great hearse stands slightly south of west; facing east he holds the *[posthumous-title]* document while the Director of Astronomy bears the lament document standing behind.
translations.idiomatic: Ritual ushers seat the Grand Commandant west of center; the hearse is angled slightly south of due west; east-facing, he lifts the posthumous-title edict as the court astrologer, behind him, grips the elegiac proclamation.

sentences.zh: 太常跪曰「進」，皇帝進。

translations.literal: The Minister of Ceremonies kneels and says “Advance”; the emperor advances.
translations.idiomatic: The Minister of Ceremonies kneels with the command “Advance,” and the sovereign steps forward.

sentences.zh: 太尉讀謚策，藏金匱。

translations.literal: The Grand Commandant reads the posthumous-title document and stores it in a golden coffer.
translations.idiomatic: He reads the temple-style rescript aloud, then locks the text inside a gilt casket.

sentences.zh: 皇帝次科藏於廟。

translations.literal: The emperor next arranges the stored items in the temple.
translations.idiomatic: The Son of Heaven then catalogs the deposited tablets and silks within the ancestral shrine.

sentences.zh: 太史奉哀策葦篋詣陵。

translations.literal: The Director of Astronomy bears the lament document in a reed basket to the mausoleum.
translations.idiomatic: The Director of Astronomy carries the elegy, boxed in wicker, toward the tomb park.

sentences.zh: 太尉旋復公位，再拜立*

translations.literal: The Grand Commandant circles back to his seat among the three dukes, twice bows with a forehead knock, and stands *
translations.idiomatic: The Grand Commandant returns to his rank with the three dukes, performs a second double-kowtow, and holds his posture—

translations.literal: Marginal gloss reads ku 哭 (weep).
translations.idiomatic: The apparatus inserts the verb “weep” at the lacuna.

translations.literal: * before the period.
translations.idiomatic: —closing the editorial asterisk before the full stop.

sentences.zh: 太常跪曰「哭」，大鴻臚傳哭，十五舉音，止哭。

translations.literal: The Minister of Ceremonies kneels and says “Weep”; the Grand Herald of Guests relays the cry; fifteen ululations sound, then weeping ceases.
translations.idiomatic: On the signal “Weep” from the Minister of Ceremonies, relayed by the Grand Herald, the assembly gives fifteen prescribed wails and then falls silent.

sentences.zh: 太常行遣奠皆如禮。

translations.literal: The Minister of Ceremonies conducts the farewell libations entirely according to the rites.
translations.idiomatic: The Minister of Ceremonies presides over every farewell offering in canonical order.

sentences.zh: 請哭止哭如儀。

translations.literal: They request weeping and cessation of weeping according to the observances.
translations.idiomatic: Starts and stops of lamentation follow the liturgical script.

sentences.zh: 注[一]周禮曰：「方相氏，大喪先柩，及墓入壙，以戈擊四隅，*

translations.literal: Comment [1] *Zhou li* says: “The *fangxiang* officer, at a great funeral, goes before the bier; reaching the tomb he enters the vault and with a spear strikes the four corners, *
translations.idiomatic: Note [1] — *Rites of Zhou*: “The exorcist precedes the catafalque on a state funeral; at the grave he descends into the chamber and strikes each corner with a halberd to—

translations.literal: Marginal gloss reads ou 毆 (strike).
translations.idiomatic: Editors gloss the verb as ou 毆, “to strike.”

translations.literal: **drive off]* the *fangliang* spirits.”
translations.idiomatic: —drive away the *fangliang* demons.”

sentences.zh: 」鄭玄曰：「方相，放想也，可畏怖之貌。

translations.literal: " Zheng Xuan says: "‘Fangxiang’ means an appearance imagined (*fangxiang*), a form fearsome to behold.
translations.idiomatic: Zheng Xuan explains: “*Fangxiang* depicts a face conjured in the mind—something terrifying to see.”

sentences.zh: 壙，穿地中也。

translations.literal: " *Kuang* means boring into the earth.
translations.idiomatic: “*Kuang*” is the hollow cut into the ground.

sentences.zh: 方良，罔兩也。

translations.literal: " *Fangliang* is the same as *wangliang*."
translations.idiomatic: “*Fangliang*” is another name for the *wangliang* goblin.

sentences.zh: 天子之幟，柏，黃腸為裡，表以石焉。

translations.literal: The Son of Heaven’s banner staff is cypress; yellow-heart oak forms the core; the surface is faced with stone.
translations.idiomatic: The imperial mortuary pole is cypress wood lined with yellow-heart timber and sheathed in stone facing.

sentences.zh: 國語曰『木石之怪夔、罔兩』。」

translations.literal: " *Guo yu* says, “Among the monsters of wood and stone are *kui* and *wangliang*.”"
translations.idiomatic: The *Discourses of the States* adds: “Spirits born of wood and rock include *kui* and *wangliang*.”

sentences.zh: 晝漏上水，請發。

translations.literal: At the clepsydra’s day division they request the cortège to depart.
translations.idiomatic: When the day watch is sounded, officers petition to set the procession moving.

sentences.zh: 司徒、河南尹先引車轉，太常跪曰「請拜送」。

translations.literal: The Minister of Education and the Governor of Henan first turn the vehicles about; the Minister of Ceremonies kneels and says, “We beg leave to bow and escort.”
translations.idiomatic: The Minister of Education and the Henan intendant pivot the train; the Minister of Ceremonies kneels with the formula, “We ask permission to bow and send off the bier.”

sentences.zh: 載車著白系參繆紼，長三十丈，大七寸為挽，六行，行五十人。

translations.literal: The hearse is tied with white cords in triple twisted mourning tassels thirty *zhang* long; the main tow-rope is seven inches thick; six ranks, fifty men each.
translations.idiomatic: White hemp in triple-plaited mourning bonds—thirty *zhang* in length—girds the hearse; the primary hawser measures seven inches; six files of fifty pullers each.

sentences.zh: 公卿以下子弟凡三百人，皆素幘委貌冠，衣素裳。

translations.literal: Sons and younger kin of grandees downward, three hundred in all, wear plain kerchiefs and *weimao* caps with white lower garments.
translations.idiomatic: Three hundred junior kinsmen of officials at rank three and below don unbleached kerchiefs, *weimao* headgear, and white skirts.

sentences.zh: 校尉三*[百]*人，皆赤幘不冠，絳科單衣，持幢幡。

translations.literal: Three *[hundred]* commandants of columns wear red kerchiefs without caps, crimson-collared unlined jackets, and carry streamers.
translations.idiomatic: Three hundred column commanders—editors mark the numeral—wear scarlet headcloths without formal caps, carmine-collared single-layer robes, and bear pennants.

sentences.zh: 候司馬丞為行首，皆銜枚。

translations.literal: The assistant commandant of the escort guard heads each file; all hold mouth-gags.
translations.idiomatic: The deputy marshal of the guard forms the head of each rank; every man keeps a wooden bit between his teeth for silence.

sentences.zh: 羽林孤兒、巴俞擢歌者六十人，為六列。

translations.literal: Sixty guardsmen-orphans of the Feather Forest and Ba-yu acrobatic singers form six columns.
translations.idiomatic: Sixty Feather-Forest cadets and Ba-yu tumblers fall into six marching files.

sentences.zh: 鐸司馬八人，執鐸先。

translations.literal: Eight bell-marshals of horse carry hand-bells and lead the way.
translations.idiomatic: Eight horse-bell sergeants with clappers walk at the van.

sentences.zh: 大鴻臚設九賓，隨立陵南羨門道東，北面；

translations.literal: The Grand Herald of Guests arrays the nine guest-delegations; they stand east of the vaulted passage south of the mound, facing north;
translations.idiomatic: The Grand Herald stations the nine guest groups along the eastern gallery of the southern ramp, all facing north;

sentences.zh: 諸侯、王公、特進道西，北面東上；

translations.literal: feudatories, kings and dukes, and specially advanced nobles stand west of the passage, facing north with the east as senior;
translations.idiomatic: feudatory lords, royal dukes, and nobles of special advancement line the western side of the ramp, north-facing, seniority running from the east;

sentences.zh: 中二千石、二千石、列侯*

translations.literal: full marquises at attendant two-thousand-*shi*, two-thousand-*shi*, and listed marquises *
translations.idiomatic: attendant two-thousand-*shi*, plain two-thousand-*shi*, and titular marquises—

translations.literal: (Yi)
translations.idiomatic: A variant gloss reads yi 宜.

sentences.zh: **[直]*九賓東，北面西上。

translations.literal: **standing as]* the nine guests on the east, facing north with the west as senior.
translations.idiomatic: —serve directly as the nine guest rows on the east, facing north, seniority counted from the west.

sentences.zh: 皇帝白布幕素裡，夾羨道東，西向如禮。

translations.literal: The emperor [sits] in a white cloth screen with plain lining east of the vaulted passage, west-facing according to the rites.
translations.idiomatic: The sovereign sits within a white linen pavilion, plain-lined, east of the gallery, facing west as canon demands.

sentences.zh: 容車幄坐羨道西，南向，車當坐，南向，中黃門尚衣奉衣就幄坐。

translations.literal: The guest hearse canopy and seat are west of the vaulted passage, south-facing; the carriage aligns with the seat, south-facing; chief eunuchs of the wardrobe bring garments to the curtained seat.
translations.idiomatic: The guest coach’s awning and chair occupy the gallery’s west side, opening south; the vehicle squares with the seat, also south-facing; wardrobe eunuchs lay silks on the dais inside the curtains.

sentences.zh: 車少前，太祝進醴獻如禮。

translations.literal: The chariot inches forward; the Grand Invocator advances with sweet-wine offerings as in the rites.
translations.idiomatic: The hearse rolls slightly forward while the Grand Invocator presents the libation of clear ale in prescribed form.

sentences.zh: 司徒跪曰「大駕請捨」，太史令自車南，北面讀哀策，掌故在後，已哀哭。

translations.literal: The Minister of Education kneels and says, “The great train begs to alight”; the Director of Astronomy comes from the south of the chariot, faces north, reads the lament document, with archivists behind him; then bitter weeping.
translations.idiomatic: The Minister of Education kneels: “The cortège asks leave to dismount.” The Director of Astronomy steps from the carriage’s south side, faces north, reads the elegy while clerks follow, and grief breaks out anew.

sentences.zh: 太常跪曰「哭」，大鴻臚傳哭如儀。

translations.literal: The Minister of Ceremonies kneels and says “Weep”; the Grand Herald relays the weeping as in the observances.
translations.idiomatic: At the cry “Weep” from the Minister of Ceremonies, the Grand Herald relays the lament through the ranks.

sentences.zh: 司徒跪曰「請就下位」，東園武士奉下車。

translations.literal: The Minister of Education kneels and says, “We beg to move to the lower station”; Eastern Park guards lift the carriage down.
translations.idiomatic: The Minister of Education petitions, “We ask to descend to the lower platform,” and Eastern Workshop bearers lower the coach.

sentences.zh: 司徒跪曰「請就下房」，都導東園武士奉車入房。

translations.literal: The Minister of Education kneels and says, “We beg to enter the lower chamber”; the chief usher leads Eastern Park guards to wheel the carriage into the chamber.
translations.idiomatic: He next requests, “We ask to enter the lower chamber,” whereupon ushers guide the guards wheeling the hearse indoors.

sentences.zh: 司徒、太史令奉謚、哀策。

translations.literal: The Minister of Education and the Director of Astronomy jointly bear the posthumous-title and lament documents.
translations.idiomatic: Minister of Education and court astrologer together carry the posthumous scroll and the elegy.
Editorial marker for note [1] following.

sentences.zh: 注[一]晉時有人嵩高山下得竹簡一枚，上有兩行科斗書之，台中外傳以相示，莫有知者。

translations.literal: Comment [1] In Jin times someone found on Mount Song a bamboo slip with two lines of tadpole script; officials inside and outside the capital passed it around, yet none could read it.
translations.idiomatic: Note [1] — During the Jin a traveler on Mount Song picked up a bamboo strip inscribed in two lines of “tadpole” seal script; it circulated through court and capital, but no scholar could decipher it.

sentences.zh: 司空張華以問博士束□。

translations.literal: Minister of Works Zhang Hua questioned the erudite Shu □ about it.
translations.idiomatic: Minister of Works Zhang Hua brought the slip to Erudite Shu—personal name missing in the text.

sentences.zh: □曰：「此明帝顯節陵中策也。

translations.literal: □ said: “This is the lament document from Emperor Ming’s Xianjie Mausoleum.
translations.idiomatic: The scholar replied: “This is the funeral elegy buried with Emperor Ming at the Xianjie tumulus.”

sentences.zh: 」檢校果然。

translations.literal: " When checked, it was indeed so.
translations.idiomatic: When archivists compared it with the archives, the match was exact.

sentences.zh: 是知策用此書也。

translations.literal: " Thus we know the documents used this script.
translations.idiomatic: Hence we learn that such texts were written in this archaic hand.

sentences.zh: 東園武士執事下明器。

translations.literal: Eastern Park guards officiate in lowering the grave goods.
translations.idiomatic: Workshop guards supervise the lowering of spirit utensils into the shaft.

sentences.zh: [一]筲八盛，容三升，[二]黍一，稷一，麥一，粱一，稻一，麻一，菽一，小豆一。

translations.literal: [1] Eight bamboo baskets, each holding three *sheng*; [2] one of glutinous millet, one of setaria millet, one of wheat, one of fine millet, one of rice, one of hemp seed, one of beans, one of small beans.
translations.idiomatic: [1] Eight shallow baskets, three *sheng* apiece; [2] separate measures of glutinous millet, foxtail millet, wheat, panicled millet, rice, hemp, beans, and adzuki beans.

sentences.zh: 甕三，容三升，醯一，醢一，屑一。

translations.literal: Three jars, each three *sheng*: one of vinegar, one of minced relish, one of spiced crumbs.
translations.idiomatic: Three earthen jars of three *sheng* each hold vinegar, hashed relish, and aromatic scrapings.

sentences.zh: [三]黍飴。

translations.literal: [3] Glutinous millet malt sugar.
translations.idiomatic: [3] A portion of malt syrup from glutinous millet.

sentences.zh: 載以木桁，覆以疏布。

translations.literal: They are carried on wooden stretchers and covered with open-weave cloth.
translations.idiomatic: Porters bear them on wooden biers veiled in coarse sackcloth.

sentences.zh: 甒二，容三升，醴一，酒一。

translations.literal: Two urns, three *sheng* each: one of sweet ale, one of wine.
translations.idiomatic: Two larger jars, again three *sheng*, contain sweet must and fermented wine.

sentences.zh: 載以木桁，覆以功布。

translations.literal: They are carried on wooden stretchers and covered with “merit” cloth.
translations.idiomatic: The same stretchers are draped this time with finer “merit” hemp.

sentences.zh: 瓦鐙一。

translations.literal: One pottery lamp.
translations.idiomatic: A single ceramic lamp for the tomb.

sentences.zh: 彤矢四，軒輖中，亦短□。

translations.literal: Four cinnabar-painted arrows, shafts “in the chariot-nave center,” likewise short □.
translations.idiomatic: Four vermilion-fletched shafts sized for the nave compartment—tips damaged in the manuscript.

sentences.zh: 彤矢四，骨，短□。

translations.literal: Four cinnabar-painted arrows, bone heads, short □.
translations.idiomatic: Four more vermilion arrows with bone points and shortened shafts—lacuna in text.

sentences.zh: [四]彤弓一。

translations.literal: [4] One cinnabar-painted bow.
translations.idiomatic: [4] One lacquered red bow to match the arrows.

sentences.zh: 琶八，牟八，[五]豆八，籩八，形方酒壺八。

translations.literal: Eight *pi* lutes, eight *mou* bowls, [5] eight bean stands, eight bamboo trays, eight square wine jars.
translations.idiomatic: Eight pear-shaped lutes, eight tureen bowls, [5] eight stem-cups, eight bamboo platters, and eight square decanters.

sentences.zh: 盤匜一具。

translations.literal: One set of wash basin and pourer.
translations.idiomatic: A matched basin and ewer for ablutions.

sentences.zh: [六]杖、幾各一。

translations.literal: [6] One staff and one low table each.
translations.idiomatic: [6] One walking stick and one arm-rest apiece.

sentences.zh: 蓋一。

translations.literal: One umbrella cover.
translations.idiomatic: A single parasol frame for shade in the otherworld.

sentences.zh: 鐘十六，無虡。

translations.literal: Sixteen bells without stands.
translations.idiomatic: Sixteen bronze bells laid on the ground without *ju* frames.

sentences.zh: 鎛四，無虡。

translations.literal: Four *bo* bells without stands.
translations.idiomatic: Four large *bo* chimes likewise left unstaged.

sentences.zh: [七]磬十六，無虡。

translations.literal: [7] Sixteen chime-stones without stands.
translations.idiomatic: [7] Sixteen lithophones without suspension racks.

sentences.zh: [八]塤一，簫四，笙一，箎一，柷一，敔一，瑟六，琴一，竽一，築一，坎侯一。

translations.literal: [8] One globular flute, four panpipes, one mouth-organ, one chi flute, one wooden clapper, one scraper, six se zithers, one qin, one large mouth-organ, one zhu zither, one *kanhou* resonator.
translations.idiomatic: [8] A full ghost orchestra: globular ocarina, panpipes, sheng, chi, *zhu* starter, *yu* stopper, six *se*, one *qin*, one *yu*, one *zhu*, and a *kanhou* bell-tree.

sentences.zh: [九]干、戈各一，笮一，甲一，冑一。

translations.literal: [9] One shield and one spear each, one rack, one suit of armour, one helmet.
translations.idiomatic: [9] Paired ritual arms: shield, spear, rack, lamellar coat, and helm.

sentences.zh: [一０]挽車九乘，芻靈三十六匹。

translations.literal: [10] Nine hearse carts and thirty-six straw horse effigies.
translations.idiomatic: [10] Nine tow-wagons plus thirty-six straw horses for the tomb escort.

sentences.zh: [一一]瓦醋二，瓦釜二，瓦甑一。

translations.literal: [11] Two pottery vinegar jars, two pottery cauldrons, one pottery steamer.
translations.idiomatic: [11] Kitchenware for the shades: two vinegar pots, two kettles, one steamer.

sentences.zh: 瓦鼎十二，容五升。

translations.literal: Twelve pottery tripods, five *sheng* capacity each.
translations.idiomatic: A dozen earthen tripods, each holding five *sheng*.

sentences.zh: 匏勺一，容一升。

translations.literal: One gourd ladle, one *sheng* capacity.
translations.idiomatic: A single calabash dipper of one *sheng*.

sentences.zh: 瓦案九。

translations.literal: Nine pottery trays.
translations.idiomatic: Nine low serving tables of unglazed ware.

sentences.zh: 瓦大杯十六，容三升。

translations.literal: Sixteen large pottery cups, three *sheng* each.
translations.idiomatic: Sixteen great drinking bowls of three *sheng*.

sentences.zh: 瓦小杯二十，容二升。

translations.literal: Twenty small pottery cups, two *sheng* each.
translations.idiomatic: Twenty modest cups of two *sheng*.

sentences.zh: 瓦飯盤十。

translations.literal: Ten pottery rice plates.
translations.idiomatic: Ten shallow rice dishes.

sentences.zh: 瓦酒樽二，容五斗。

translations.literal: Two pottery wine jars, five *dou* each.
translations.idiomatic: Two wine jars of five *dou* capacity.

sentences.zh: 匏勺二，容一升。

translations.literal: Two gourd ladles, one *sheng* each.
translations.idiomatic: Two more gourd scoops, one *sheng* apiece.

sentences.zh: 注[一]禮記曰：「明器，神明之也。

translations.literal: Comment [1] *Record of Rites* says: "Spirit goods are for the spirits.
translations.idiomatic: Note [1] — *Book of Rites*: “Spirit utensils belong to the world of shades.”

sentences.zh: 孔子謂為明器知喪道矣，備物而不可用也。

translations.literal: Confucius said that making spirit goods showed understanding of mourning: complete in appearance yet unusable.
translations.idiomatic: Confucius judged such replicas proof that one grasps funeral doctrine: every form supplied, yet nothing functional.

sentences.zh: 」鄭玄注既夕曰：「陳明器，以西行南端為上。」

translations.literal: " Zheng Xuan’s commentary on *Ji xi* says: "When arraying spirit goods, rank them in lines toward the west with the southern end honored."
translations.idiomatic: Zheng Xuan’s gloss on *Evening Burial* adds: “Lay the grave goods out in westward files, giving precedence to the southern end.”

sentences.zh: 注[二]鄭玄注既夕曰：「筲，畚種類也，其容蓋與簋同。」

translations.literal: Comment [2] Zheng Xuan’s commentary on *Ji xi* says: "Baskets are of the dustpan class; their capacity should match that of a *gui* bowl."
translations.idiomatic: Note [2] — Zheng Xuan on *Evening Burial*: “These shallow baskets resemble winnowing pans; their volume equals a standard *gui*.”

sentences.zh: 注[三]鄭玄注既夕曰：「屑，姜桂之屑。」

translations.literal: Comment [3] Zheng Xuan’s commentary on *Ji xi* says: "Crumbs means shredded ginger and cassia."
translations.idiomatic: Note [3] — Zheng Xuan: “The ‘scrapings’ are shaved ginger and cinnamon.”

sentences.zh: 注[四]既夕曰：「翭矢一乘，骨鏃短□。

translations.literal: Comment [4] *Ji xi* says: "One team of *hou* arrows, bone heads, short □.
translations.idiomatic: Note [4] — *Evening Burial*: “One quiver of *hou* arrows with bone points and shortened shafts—

sentences.zh: 」鄭玄曰：「翭猶候也，候物而射之矢也。

translations.literal: " Zheng Xuan says: "‘Hou’ means waiting; arrows that wait on a target before release.
translations.idiomatic: Zheng Xuan glosses *hou* as ‘watching’—missiles that hover for their mark.

sentences.zh: 四矢曰乘。

translations.literal: " Four arrows make one team.
translations.idiomatic: Four shafts constitute one “team.”

sentences.zh: 骨鏃短□，亦示不用也。

translations.literal: " Bone heads and short □ likewise show they are not for use.
translations.idiomatic: Bone tips and stub shafts likewise signal that they must never be shot.

sentences.zh: 生時翭矢金鏃，凡為矢，五分笴長而羽其一。

translations.literal: " In life *hou* arrows had metal heads; for any arrow the feathers are one-fifth the shaft length.
translations.idiomatic: Living archery employed bronze-headed *hou* shafts; by rule the fletching equals one-fifth of the bamboo length.

sentences.zh: 」通俗文曰：「細毛翭也。」

translations.literal: " *Su su wen* says: "Fine down is called *hou*."
translations.idiomatic: The *Popular Explanations* adds: “Soft down feathers are called *hou*.”

sentences.zh: 注[五]鄭玄注既夕曰：「牟，盛湯漿。」

translations.literal: Comment [5] Zheng Xuan’s commentary on *Ji xi* says: "The *mou* vessel holds broth and gruel."
translations.idiomatic: Note [5] — Zheng Xuan: “The *mou* jar is for soups and rice gruel.”

sentences.zh: 注[六]鄭玄注既夕曰：「盤匜，盥器也。」

translations.literal: Comment [6] Zheng Xuan’s commentary on *Ji xi* says: "Basin and pourer are lavatory vessels."
translations.idiomatic: Note [6] — Zheng Xuan: “The basin and ewer pair are hand-washing implements.”

sentences.zh: 注[七]爾雅曰：「大鐘謂之鏞。

translations.literal: Comment [7] *Erya* says: "A great bell is called *yong*.
translations.idiomatic: Note [7] — *Erya*: “A large bell is named *yong*.”

sentences.zh: 」郭璞注曰：「書曰『笙鏞以閒』。

translations.literal: " Guo Pu’s commentary says: "The *Documents* reads ‘sheng and *yong* in alternation.’
translations.idiomatic: Guo Pu cites the *Canon of Documents*: “The mouth-organs and great bells answer one another.”

sentences.zh: 亦名鎛。」

translations.literal: " It is also named *bo*."
translations.idiomatic: That instrument is likewise called *bo*.”

sentences.zh: 注[八]禮記曰：「有鐘磬而無簨虡。

translations.literal: Comment [8] *Record of Rites* says: "There may be bells and chimes but no *sun* or *ju* stands.
translations.idiomatic: Note [8] — *Book of Rites*: “You may furnish bells and lithophones, yet supply no hanging frames.”

sentences.zh: 」鄭玄曰：「不懸之也。」

translations.literal: " Zheng Xuan says: "They are not suspended."
translations.idiomatic: Zheng Xuan explains: “They are left unstaged on the floor.”

sentences.zh: 注[九]禮記曰：「琴瑟張而不平，竽笙備而不和。」

translations.literal: Comment [9] *Record of Rites* says: "Zithers and *se* are strung but not tuned; mouth-organs and *sheng* are complete but not brought into harmony."
translations.idiomatic: Note [9] — *Book of Rites*: “The *qin* and *se* are mounted yet left untuned; *yu* and *sheng* are fully assembled yet never played in concert.”

sentences.zh: 注[一０]既夕謂之役器。

translations.literal: Comment [10] *Ji xi* calls them "service implements."
translations.idiomatic: Note [10] — *Evening Burial* classifies these as “implements for the dead man’s service.”

sentences.zh: 鄭玄曰：「笮，矢箙。」

translations.literal: Zheng Xuan says: "The *zha* is the arrow quiver."
translations.idiomatic: Zheng Xuan glosses *zha* as the leather tube that holds arrows.

sentences.zh: 注[一一]鄭玄注禮記曰：「芻靈，東茅為人馬，謂之芻靈，神之類。」

translations.literal: Comment [11] Zheng Xuan’s commentary on *Record of Rites* says: "Straw effigies are men and horses twisted from eastern rushes; they are called straw effigies, a class of spirit things."
translations.idiomatic: Note [11] — Zheng Xuan: “*Chu ling* figures are rush-woven men and horses; they belong to the same order of ghost furnishings.”

sentences.zh: 祭服衣送皆畢，東園匠曰「可哭」，在房中者皆哭。

translations.literal: When sacrifice garments and the escort of clothing are finished, the Eastern Park artisan says "You may weep"; all inside the chamber weep.
translations.idiomatic: Once the grave clothes have been sent off, the foreman of the Eastern Workshop calls, “Weep,” and everyone within the chamber breaks into lament.

sentences.zh: 太常、大鴻臚請哭止*[哭]*如儀。

translations.literal: The Minister of Ceremonies and the Grand Herald of Guests request weeping to cease *[weeping]* according to the observances.
translations.idiomatic: The Minister of Ceremonies and the Grand Herald then petition—editors repeat the word “weep”—to end the ululation on cue.

sentences.zh: 司徒曰「百官事畢，臣請罷」，從入房者皆再拜，出，就位。

translations.literal: The Minister of Education says, "The hundred officials’ business is finished; your servant begs to dismiss them"; those who followed into the chamber all twice bow, leave, and take their stations.
translations.idiomatic: The Minister of Education announces, “All offices have discharged their duties; I ask leave to release them,” whereupon everyone who entered the room performs a double obeisance, withdraws, and resumes formation outside.

sentences.zh: 太常導皇帝就贈位。

translations.literal: The Minister of Ceremonies guides the emperor to the position for grave-goods offerings.
translations.idiomatic: The Minister of Ceremonies escorts the sovereign to the spot from which mortuary gifts are cast.

sentences.zh: 司徒跪曰「請進贈」，侍中奉持鴻洞。

translations.literal: The Minister of Education kneels and says, "We beg to advance the offerings"; the palace attendant holds the vertical offering shaft (*hongdong*).
translations.idiomatic: The Minister of Education kneels: “We ask to present the offerings,” while a chamberlain steadies the deep offering chute.

sentences.zh: 贈王珪長尺四寸，薦以紫巾，廣袤各三寸，緹裡，赤纁周緣；

translations.literal: The jade tablet offered to the king is one foot four inches long, presented on a purple cloth three inches square each way, orange silk lining, crimson *xun* silk binding round the edge;
translations.idiomatic: The gift *gui* measures fourteen inches, cradled on a violet square napkin three inches to a side, lined with orange silk and edged with a band of scarlet *xun*;

sentences.zh: 贈幣，玄三纁二，各長尺二寸，廣充幅。

translations.literal: the silk rolls offered are three black and two crimson, each one foot two inches long, width equal to a full bolt.
translations.idiomatic: the accompanying bolts—three black, two red—are each twelve inches long and as wide as a standard piece.

sentences.zh: 皇帝進跪，臨羨道房戶，西向，手下贈，投鴻洞中，三。

translations.literal: The emperor advances, kneels at the door of the tunnel chamber facing west, lowers the offerings by hand, and casts them into the *hongdong* three times.
translations.idiomatic: The sovereign steps forward, kneels at the gallery door with his back to the east, and three times drops the gifts down the stone shaft.

sentences.zh: 東園匠奉封入藏房中。

translations.literal: Eastern Park artisans receive the sealed bundles and store them inside the chamber.
translations.idiomatic: Workshop craftsmen take the wrapped offerings and seal them away in the vault.

sentences.zh: 太常跪曰「皇帝敬再拜，請哭」，大鴻臚傳哭如儀。

translations.literal: The Minister of Ceremonies kneels and says, "The emperor respectfully twice bows; we beg to weep"; the Grand Herald relays the weeping as in the observances.
translations.idiomatic: The Minister of Ceremonies intones, “The Son of Heaven bows twice; we ask leave to lament,” and the Grand Herald passes the cry through the ranks.

sentences.zh: 太常跪曰「贈事畢」，皇帝促就位。

translations.literal: The Minister of Ceremonies kneels and says, "The offering business is finished"; the emperor is urged back to his station.
translations.idiomatic: When the Minister of Ceremonies declares the offerings complete, attendants hurry the sovereign to his appointed place.

sentences.zh: [一]容根車游載容衣。

translations.literal: [1] The guest-rootwood coach carries the touring garments in state.
translations.idiomatic: [1] The root-wood guest carriage bears the touring wardrobe for display.

sentences.zh: 司徒至便殿，並□騎皆從容車玉帳下。

translations.literal: The Minister of Education reaches the side hall; □ mounted escorts all follow beneath the guest coach’s jade canopy.
translations.idiomatic: The Minister of Education withdraws to the annex, while cavalry escorts—one graph missing—fall in under the hearse’s jade awning.

sentences.zh: 司徒跪曰「請就幄」，導登。

translations.literal: The Minister of Education kneels and says, "We beg to enter the canopy"; ushers conduct him up.
translations.idiomatic: He kneels again—“We ask to mount the pavilion”—and conductors help him ascend.

sentences.zh: 尚衣奉衣，以次奉器衣物，藏於便殿。

translations.literal: Wardrobe officials present garments, then in sequence present vessels and clothing, storing them in the side hall.
translations.idiomatic: Palace wardrobe eunuchs hand up silks, then utensils and further vestments, which are laid away in the annex.

sentences.zh: 太祝進醴獻。

translations.literal: The Grand Invocator advances with the sweet-wine libation.
translations.idiomatic: The Grand Invocator offers the ritual ale.

sentences.zh: 凡下，用漏十刻。

translations.literal: For every descent ten clepsydra marks are used.
translations.idiomatic: Each lowering of the catafalque is timed to ten divisions of the water clock.

sentences.zh: 禮畢，司空將校復土。

translations.literal: When the rites finish, the Minister of Works leads engineers to backfill the tomb.
translations.idiomatic: Once liturgy ends, the Minister of Works supervises the filling of the shaft.

sentences.zh: 注[一]續漢書曰：「明帝崩，司徒鮑昱典喪事，葬日，三公入安梓宮，還，至羨道半，逢上欲下，昱前叩頭言：『禮，天子鴻洞以贈，所以重郊廟也。

translations.literal: Comment [1] *Xu Han shu* says: "When Emperor Ming died, Minister of Education Bao Yu directed the funeral; on burial day the three dukes entered to steady the inner coffin, and returning, halfway along the vaulted ramp they met the sovereign wishing to descend; Yu stepped forward, knocked his head, and said, ‘By ritual the Son of Heaven casts grave goods through the *hongdong* to honor suburban altars and temples.
translations.idiomatic: Note [1] — *Continued Book of Later Han* records Emperor Ming’s obsequies: Minister of Education Bao Yu superintended the lying-in-state; as the three dukes steadied the catafalque and turned back, they met the emperor halfway down the ramp, about to climb into the offering shaft. Bao Yu threw himself forward and said, “Canon requires the sovereign to drop mortuary gifts through the *hongdong* so that suburban and ancestral shrines retain their majesty.

sentences.zh: 陛下柰何冒危險，不以義割哀？

translations.literal: Why would Your Majesty brave such danger and refuse to restrain grief by duty?"
translations.idiomatic: Why court peril and refuse to bridle sorrow with righteousness?”

sentences.zh: 』上即還。」

translations.literal: " The sovereign at once turned back."
translations.idiomatic: The emperor immediately withdrew.”

sentences.zh: 皇帝、皇后以下皆去麤服，服大紅，還宮反廬，立主如禮。

translations.literal: The emperor, empress, and all downward remove coarse mourning and don great *hong*, return to the palace and the mourning hut, and set up the spirit tablet according to the rites.
translations.idiomatic: From the Son of Heaven and empress downward, mourners strip rough hemp and don the heavier *hong* robe, re-enter the palace and the reversed hut, and install the spirit tablet in canonical form.

sentences.zh: 桑木主尺二寸，不書謚。

translations.literal: The mulwood spirit tablet is one foot two inches long and bears no posthumous title.
translations.idiomatic: The interim tablet of mulberry measures twelve inches and carries no temple name.

sentences.zh: 虞禮畢，祔於廟，如禮。

translations.literal: When the *yu* rites are finished, it is joined in the temple according to the observances.
translations.idiomatic: After the *yu* appeasement, the tablet is enshrined with the ancestors as ritual prescribes.

sentences.zh: [一] 注[一]漢舊儀曰：「高帝崩三日，小斂室中□下。

translations.literal: [1] Comment [1] *Han ji yi* says: "Three days after Gaozu’s death the lesser laying-in took place in the chamber □ below.
translations.idiomatic: [1] Note [1] — *Han Court Ceremonial*: “On the third day after Gaozu died the lesser enshrouding was held in the inner room—one character missing—below.”

sentences.zh: 作栗木主，長八寸，前方後圓，圍一尺，置□中，望外，內張撓絮以鄣外，以皓木大如指，長三尺，四枚，纏以皓皮四方置□中，主居其中央。

translations.literal: They fashioned a chestnut spirit tablet eight inches long, square in front and round behind, one *chi* in girth, placed in the □ facing outward, padded inside with twisted floss to screen the outside; four *hao* sticks thick as a finger and three *chi* long, wrapped in *hao* bark, were set at the four quarters inside the □, the tablet occupying the center.
translations.idiomatic: A chestnut tablet eight inches long—square brow, round heel, one *chi* around—was set in the casket niche facing out, the interior stuffed with wadded floss; four finger-thick *hao* pegs three *chi* long, swathed in *hao* bark, framed the niche while the tablet stood in the middle.

sentences.zh: 七日大斂棺，以黍飯羊舌祭之□中。

translations.literal: On the seventh day the great laying-in closed the outer coffin; glutinous millet and a sheep’s tongue were offered in the □.
translations.idiomatic: On the seventh day the great enshrouding sealed the outer shell, with a sacrifice of glutinous rice and a sheep’s tongue in the same niche.

sentences.zh: 已葬，收主。

translations.literal: After burial the tablet was taken in.
translations.idiomatic: Once the tumulus was closed, the spirit board was recovered.

sentences.zh: 為木函，藏廟太室中西牆壁埳中，望內，外不出室堂之上。

translations.literal: A wooden case was made and hidden in a pit in the west wall of the Grand Chamber of the temple, facing inward, not emerging above the hall floor.
translations.idiomatic: It was boxed in timber and sealed in a cavity in the Grand Chamber’s west wall, the face turned inward so nothing protruded into the hall.

sentences.zh: 坐為五時衣、冠、履，幾、杖、竹籠。

translations.literal: Seated spirit outfits—seasonal robes, caps, shoes, arm-rest, staff, and bamboo basket—were provided.
translations.idiomatic: For the seated shade they supplied seasonal dress, footwear, cane, low table, and a bamboo hamper.

sentences.zh: 為俑人，無頭，坐起如生時。

translations.literal: Terracotta attendants without heads were made to sit and stand as in life.
translations.idiomatic: Clay figurines, deliberately headless, were posed sitting and standing as the deceased had lived.

sentences.zh: 皇后主長七寸，圍九寸，在皇帝主右旁。

translations.literal: The empress’s tablet was seven inches long, nine inches around, standing to the right of the emperor’s tablet.
translations.idiomatic: The empress’s spirit slip measured seven inches in height and nine in circumference, placed to the right of the sovereign’s.

sentences.zh: 高皇帝主長九寸。

translations.literal: The High Founder’s tablet was nine inches long.
translations.idiomatic: Gaozu’s tablet stood nine inches high.

sentences.zh: 上林給栗木，長安祠廟作神主，東園秘器作梓棺，素木長丈三尺，崇廣四尺。」

translations.literal: " The Shanglin Park supplied chestnut timber; Chang’an’s shrines fashioned the tablets; the Eastern Park’s secret coffers produced a catalpa outer shell from plain timber one *zhang* three feet long, four *chi* high and wide."
translations.idiomatic: The imperial preserve sent chestnut lumber; metropolitan shrines carved the tablets; the Eastern Workshop’s sealed coffers turned out a catalpa shell thirteen feet long and four feet square.”

sentences.zh: 先大駕日游冠衣於諸宮諸殿，腢臣皆吉服從會如儀。

translations.literal: First the great cortège tours touring caps and robes through every palace and hall; all ministers attend in auspicious dress according to the observances.
translations.idiomatic: Before the state hearse moves, touring vestments are displayed through each palace; the full bureaucracy follows in festive mourning as the code directs.

sentences.zh: 皇帝近臣喪服如禮。

translations.literal: The emperor’s intimate attendants wear mourning dress according to the rites.
translations.idiomatic: Close companions of the throne observe graded sackcloth.

sentences.zh: 醳大紅，服小紅，十一升都布練冠。

translations.literal: They lay aside great *hong* and wear lesser *hong*, with an eleven-*sheng* plain-weave cap.

translations.idiomatic: Household intimates and every officer under two thousand *shi* don the yellowish mourning kerchief.

sentences.zh: 祭以特牲，不進毛血首。

sentences.zh: 司徒、光祿勳備三爵如禮。

translations.idiomatic: Mortuary hall, park yamen, and clerks’ barracks all lie east of the axis.

sentences.zh: 堤封田十八頃十九畝三十步。

translations.literal: The enclosed field is eighteen *qing* nineteen *mu* thirty *bu*.
translations.idiomatic: The reserved land covers eighteen *qing*, nineteen *mu*, and thirty *bu*.

sentences.zh: 帝王世記曰：「在雒陽西北，去雒陽十五里。

translations.literal: *Di wang shi ji* says: "Northwest of Luoyang, fifteen *li* distant.
translations.idiomatic: The *Record of Emperors and Kings* again places it fifteen *li* northwest of the capital.

sentences.zh: 」沖帝懷陵，山方百八十三步，高四丈六尺。

translations.idiomatic: Emperor Chong’s Huailing is 183 paces square and forty-six feet high.

sentences.zh: 為寢殿行馬，四出門。

translations.idiomatic: The mourning hall is ringed by *xingma* rails opening on four sides.

translations.idiomatic: Park and temple clerks lodge east of the hall.

translations.idiomatic: The cordoned ground totals five *qing* and eighty *mu*.

translations.idiomatic: The *Record of Emperors and Kings* adds: “[Northwest of] Luoyang—fifteen *li* from the city.”

translations.literal: " Emperor Zhi’s Jing Mound is one hundred thirty-six paces square, five *zhang* five *chi* high; *xingma* barriers are used, opening four *[Sima]* gates.
translations.idiomatic: Emperor Zhi’s Jingling covers 136 paces square, rises fifty-five feet, and relies on *xingma* rails with four *Sima* portals.

translations.literal: Emperor Huan’s Xuan Mound—*Di wang shi ji* says: "The mound is three hundred paces square and twelve *zhang* high.

translations.idiomatic: It lies thirty *li* southeast of Luoyang.”

translations.literal: Emperor Ling’s Wen Mound—*Di wang shi ji* says: "The mound is three hundred paces square and twelve *zhang* high.
translations.idiomatic: Emperor Ling’s Wenling—again three hundred paces square and twelve *zhang* tall per the *Record of Emperors and Kings*.

sentences.zh: 在雒陽西北，去雒陽二十里。」

translations.literal: Northwest of Luoyang, twenty *li* from the city."
translations.idiomatic: Twenty *li* northwest of the capital.”

translations.literal: Emperor Xian’s Shan Mound—*Di wang shi ji* says: "No tumulus was raised; depth five *zhang*; front chamber one *zhang* eight feet square; rear chamber one *fang* five feet square; corner span six *chi*.
translations.idiomatic: Emperor Xian’s Shanling—*Record of Emperors and Kings*: “No surface mound; the shaft sinks fifty feet; the fore hall measures eighteen feet square, the rear fifteen, corner bays six feet across.”

sentences.zh: 在河內山陽之濁城西北，去濁城直行十一里，斜行七里，去懷陵百一十里，去山陽五十里，南去雒陽三百一十里。

translations.idiomatic: Cai Zhi’s *Han Ceremonial* notes: “The twelve imperial tomb stewards need not bow to the Henan governor.”

translations.literal: " Wei Emperor Wen’s testamentary summary says: "That Emperor Wen of Han was never robbed at Baling was because he sought nothing.
translations.idiomatic: Wei Wendi’s *Final Instructions* adds: “Wendi’s Baling stayed intact because he buried no treasure.”

sentences.zh: 光武之掘原陵，封樹也。

translations.literal: That Guangwu’s Yuanyuan was opened was because of mound trees and sealing.
translations.idiomatic: Guangwu’s Yuanyuan was rifled because of its high mound and marker trees.

sentences.zh: 霸陵之完，功在釋之；

translations.literal: Baling’s integrity owed its merit to Shi Zhi;
translations.idiomatic: Baling survived thanks to Zhang Shi’s remonstrance;

sentences.zh: 原陵之掘，罪在明帝。

translations.literal: Yuanyuan’s violation lay in Emperor Ming’s crime.
translations.idiomatic: the looting of Yuanyuan was Emperor Ming’s fault.

sentences.zh: 是釋之忠以利君，明帝愛以害親也。

translations.literal: Thus Shi Zhi’s loyalty profited his lord, while Ming’s affection harmed his kin.
translations.idiomatic: Loyalty like Shi Zhi’s benefited the throne; Ming’s indulgence injured his ancestors.

sentences.zh: 忠臣孝子，宜思釋之之言，察明帝之戒，存於所以安君定親，使魂靈萬載無危，斯則賢聖之忠孝矣。

translations.literal: Loyal ministers and filial sons ought to ponder Shi Zhi’s words, study Ming’s warning, and keep in mind how to secure ruler and kin so shades endure ten thousand generations without peril—such is the loyalty and filial piety of the worthy.
translations.idiomatic: True ministers and dutiful sons should weigh Shi Zhi’s counsel, heed Ming’s caution, and aim at whatever truly secures sovereign and family, so souls rest untroubled for ages—that is sage-like devotion.

sentences.zh: 自古及今，未有不亡之國，亦無不掘之墓也。

translations.literal: From antiquity to the present there has never been a state that did not perish, nor a tomb that was never opened.
translations.idiomatic: No dynasty has lasted forever, and no sepulcher has escaped the spade forever.

sentences.zh: 喪亂以來，漢氏諸陵無不發掘，至乃燒取玉柙金縷，骸骨並盡，是焚如之刑也，豈不重痛哉。

translations.literal: Since the disorders began, not one Han imperial tomb has avoided excavation; robbers even burned the jade shrouds to melt the gold thread, leaving bones consumed—that is the punishment of burning alive; could the pain be greater?
translations.idiomatic: After rebellion spread, every Han mausoleum was violated; thieves fired the jade suits to recover gold thread until even the bones were gone—a torment like being burned at the stake, a grief beyond words.

sentences.zh: 禍由乎厚葬封樹，桑、霍為我戒，不亦明乎！

translations.literal: The disaster stems from lavish burial and sealing trees—Sang Hongyang and Huo Guang gave us warning; is it not plain?
translations.idiomatic: The scourge arises from opulent interments and marker groves; ministers like Sang and Huo already warned us—how much clearer need it be?

translations.idiomatic: grasping death is his farthest reach.”
