translations.literal: " Those who understand life do not let things injure life;
translations.idiomatic: “Those who know how to live will not let possessions harm their lives;

sentences.zh: 知死者，不以物害死。

translations.literal: those who understand death do not let things injure death.
translations.idiomatic: those who know how to die will not let possessions harm their deaths.”

sentences.zh: 凡生於天地之閒，其必有死。

translations.literal: " All who are born between Heaven and Earth must die.
translations.idiomatic: “Whatever is born under heaven is bound to perish.”

sentences.zh: 孝子之重其親者，若親之愛其子，不棄於溝壑，故有葬送之義。

translations.literal: " Filial sons who honor parents do as parents who love children—never casting them into ditches—hence the duty of burial and send-off.
translations.idiomatic: “Filial children cherish parents the way parents cherish infants; they would never dump them in gullies, therefore burial rites exist.”

sentences.zh: 葬者，藏也。

translations.literal: " Burial means concealment.
translations.idiomatic: “To bury is to hide.”

sentences.zh: 以生人心為之慮，則莫如無動，無動莫如無利。

translations.literal: " If one plans with living men’s hearts, nothing surpasses no disturbance; nothing surpasses no profit better than no disturbance.
translations.idiomatic: “Measured by the anxious heart of the living, the best plan is to leave graves unmolested—and nothing tempts molesters like profit.”

sentences.zh: 葬淺則狐狸掘之，深則及水泉，故必高陵之上，以避二害。

translations.literal: " Bury shallow and foxes dig; bury deep and you strike the water table; hence one must choose high ridges to escape both harms.
translations.idiomatic: “Too shallow and foxes tunnel in; too deep and you flood the shaft—only a high terrace avoids both perils.”

sentences.zh: 然而忘奸寇之變，豈不惑哉！

translations.literal: " Yet forgetting the danger of villains—is that not folly?
translations.idiomatic: “Yet to forget robbers—is that not blindness?”

sentences.zh: 民之於利也，犯白刃，涉危難以求之；

translations.literal: " Commoners, for profit, will brave naked blades and cross mortal peril to seize it;
translations.idiomatic: “People will face naked steel and deadly risk for gain;

sentences.zh: 忍親戚，欺知交以求之。

translations.literal: they will wrong kin and cheat friends to seize it.
translations.idiomatic: they will betray family and swindle friends for gain.”

sentences.zh: 今無此危，無此醜，而為利甚厚，固難禁也。

translations.literal: " Here there is neither that peril nor that shame, yet the profit is enormous—how could it be forbidden?
translations.idiomatic: “Here there is no such danger, no such infamy, yet the reward is huge—of course it cannot be stopped.”

sentences.zh: 國彌大，家彌富，其葬彌厚，珠玉金銅，不可勝計。

translations.literal: " The larger the state, the richer the house, the thicker the burial—pearls, jade, gold, and bronze beyond counting.
translations.idiomatic: “The mightier the kingdom, the wealthier the clan, the heavier the grave goods—gems and bullion beyond reckoning.”

sentences.zh: 奸人聞之，轉以相告，雖有嚴刑重罪，不能止也。

translations.literal: Villains hear of it and pass the word along; though punishments be severe, they cannot be stopped.
translations.idiomatic: Rogues hear rumors and spread them; harsh laws never halt the plunder.

sentences.zh: 且死者彌久，生者彌疏，彌疏則守之彌怠。

translations.literal: " Moreover, the longer the dead lie, the more distant the living; the more distant, the lazier the watch.
translations.idiomatic: “Moreover, time widens the gap between descendants and ancestors; distance breeds neglect in guardians.”

sentences.zh: 藏器如故而守之有怠，其勢固必掘矣。

translations.literal: " The treasures remain as before while the watch slackens—excavation becomes inevitable.
translations.idiomatic: “When wealth stays intact but vigilance fades, digging is only a matter of time.”

sentences.zh: 世*

translations.literal: " From age *
translations.idiomatic: “From generation—

translations.literal: (to)
translations.idiomatic: —the gloss reads *zhi* 至, ‘until,’—

sentences.zh: **[主]*為丘隴，其高若山陵，樹之若林藪，或設闕庭、都邑。

translations.literal: **ruler]* they have heaped tumuli like mountain ranges, planted them like forests, even built gate-towers and miniature cities.
translations.idiomatic: —sovereigns have piled barrows like hills, planted groves of markers, even raised mock palaces.”

sentences.zh: 以此示富則可矣，以此為死者則惑矣！

translations.literal: " To display wealth in this way may satisfy vanity, but to do it for the dead is delusion!
translations.idiomatic: “Such display may flaunt riches, yet it helps the dead not at all.”

sentences.zh: 大凡死者，其視萬世猶一*

translations.literal: " As a rule the dead regard ten thousand generations as one *
translations.idiomatic: “To the shades, myriad ages pass like one—

translations.literal: (blink)
translations.idiomatic: —editors gloss *ming* 瞑, ‘close the eyes,’—

translations.literal: **instant]*."
translations.idiomatic: —a single blink.”

sentences.zh: 人之壽，久者不過百，中者六十。

translations.literal: " Human life at longest does not pass one hundred years; the middle span is sixty.
translations.idiomatic: “Even the longest life rarely reaches a hundred; the median is sixty.”

sentences.zh: 以百與六十為無窮者慮，其情固不相當矣。

translations.literal: " To plan for infinity on the scale of a hundred or sixty years—such feelings cannot match.
translations.idiomatic: “Yet people plan for eternity on the scale of sixty or a hundred years—how mismatched the math.”

sentences.zh: 必以無窮為慮，然後為可。

translations.literal: " Only if one plans for infinity can it be adequate.
translations.idiomatic: “Only planning for the endless truly suffices.”

sentences.zh: 今有銘其墓曰，『此中有金寶甚厚，不可掘也』，必為世笑矣。

translations.literal: " Suppose an epitaph read, ‘Gold and jewels lie here in great store—do not dig’—the world would laugh.
translations.idiomatic: “Inscribe ‘great treasure here—keep out,’ and posterity would only jeer.”

sentences.zh: 而為之闕庭以自表，此何異彼哉！

translations.literal: " Yet building gate-towers to advertise oneself—how is that different?
translations.idiomatic: “Building courtyards to boast is no wiser than such a sign.”

sentences.zh: 自古及今，未有不亡之國也。

translations.literal: " From antiquity to the present there has never been a state that did not perish.
translations.idiomatic: “No state endures forever.”

sentences.zh: 無不亡之國，是無不掘之墓。

translations.literal: " Where no state fails to perish, no tomb fails to be opened.
translations.idiomatic: “Where every realm falls, every tomb is breached.”

sentences.zh: 以耳目之所聞見，則齊、荊、燕嘗亡矣；

translations.literal: " By what eye and ear have witnessed, Qi, Jing, and Yan have perished;
translations.idiomatic: “We need only recall how Qi, Chu, and Yan vanished;

sentences.zh: 宋、中山已亡矣；

translations.literal: Song and Zhongshan are already gone;
translations.idiomatic: how Song and Zhongshan fell;

sentences.zh: 趙、韓、魏皆失其故國矣。

translations.literal: Zhao, Han, and Wei have all lost their old domains.
translations.idiomatic: how Zhao, Han, and Wei forfeited their thrones.”

sentences.zh: 自此以上，亡國不可勝數，故其大墓無不掘也。

translations.literal: " Above that level the lost states are beyond count, hence their great tombs were all opened.
translations.idiomatic: “Beyond count lie ruined kingdoms, and every one of their grand mausolea was rifled.”

sentences.zh: 而猶皆爭為之，豈不悲哉！

translations.literal: " Yet people still vie to build them—is it not pitiful?
translations.idiomatic: “Still mortals compete in lavish burial—what tragedy!”

sentences.zh: 今夫君之不令民，父之不*

translations.literal: " Now as for rulers who do not instruct the people, fathers who do not *
translations.idiomatic: “When lords fail to teach the commons, when fathers do not—

translations.literal: (teach)
translations.idiomatic: —the gloss suggests *jiao* 教—

sentences.zh: **[孝]*子，兄之不悌弟，皆鄉邑之所遺，而憚耕耒之勞者也。

translations.literal: **filial]* sons, elder brothers who are not kind to younger brothers—all are cast-offs of village and town who shun the toil of the plow.
translations.idiomatic: —raise filial sons, when elder brothers bully juniors—such folk are the dregs of hamlets, idle drones who flee the hoe.”

sentences.zh: 仍不事耕農，而好鮮衣侈食。

translations.literal: " They still refuse farming yet love fine clothes and extravagant food.
translations.idiomatic: “They refuse tillage yet crave silks and feasts.”

sentences.zh: 智巧窮匱，則合黨連觿，而謀名丘大墓。

translations.literal: " When wit and craft run dry, they band in gangs to plot famous tumuli.
translations.idiomatic: “When their tricks fail, they league together to target celebrated tombs.”

sentences.zh: 上曾不能禁也，此有葬自表之禍也。

translations.literal: " Superiors cannot stop them—this is the disaster of advertising one’s burial.
translations.idiomatic: “Magistrates cannot restrain them—this is the curse of a self-advertised grave.”

sentences.zh: 昔堯葬谷林，通樹之；

translations.literal: " Of old Yao was buried in Guilin with trees planted all around;
translations.idiomatic: “Yao lay in Guilin’s vale with trees marking the spot;

sentences.zh: 舜葬紀巿，不變肆；

translations.literal: Shun was buried at Ji Market without disturbing the market stalls;
translations.idiomatic: Shun rested at Ji Market without displacing the shops;

sentences.zh: 禹葬會稽，不變人徒。

translations.literal: Yu was buried at Kuaiji without conscripting labor.
translations.idiomatic: Yu slept at Kuaiji without impressing corvée.”

sentences.zh: 非愛其費，以為死者*[慮]*也。

translations.literal: " It was not stinginess with expense but *[consideration]* for the dead.
translations.idiomatic: “They were not miserly—they were thinking of the dead.”

sentences.zh: 先王之所惡，惡死者之辱。

translations.literal: " What the ancient kings hated was the shame of the dead being exposed.
translations.idiomatic: “What former kings loathed was the humiliation of violated corpses.”

sentences.zh: 以為儉則不發，不發則不辱，故必以儉而合乎山原也。

translations.literal: " They believed simplicity prevented opening; no opening meant no shame—hence they chose frugality suited to hills and plains.
translations.idiomatic: “They held that modest graves were never robbed; unrobbed corpses suffered no outrage—so they buried plainly on high ground.”

sentences.zh: 宋未亡而東頤掘，齊未亡而莊公*[頤]*掘。

translations.literal: " Song’s eastern tumuli were dug while Song still lived; Qi’s Duke Zhuang’s *[tomb]* was opened before Qi fell.
translations.idiomatic: “Song’s eastern barrows were rifled while Song survived; Duke Zhuang of Qi’s mound was violated before Qi perished.”

sentences.zh: 國存而乃若此，又況滅名之後乎！

translations.literal: " If it was thus while the state endured, how much more after its name was lost!
translations.idiomatic: “If such things happened under a living dynasty, what awaits a vanished one?”

sentences.zh: 此愛而厚葬之故也。

translations.literal: " This is the fruit of doting burial.
translations.idiomatic: “Thus love expressed through rich tombs becomes harm.”

sentences.zh: 欲愛而反害之，欲安而反危之，忠臣孝子亦不可以厚葬矣。

translations.literal: " Wishing to cherish yet harming, wishing to secure yet endangering—loyal ministers and filial sons must not pursue thick burial.
translations.idiomatic: “Affection that injures, care that imperils—true ministers and sons cannot endorse lavish interment.”

sentences.zh: 昔季孫以璵璠斂，孔子歷級而止之，為無窮慮也。」

translations.literal: " Once Jisun wanted to enshroud with *yufan* jades; Confucius ran up the steps to stop him, acting from concern for the endless future."
translations.idiomatic: “When Jisun planned a jade *yufan* shroud, Confucius mounted the stairs to forbid it, thinking of eternity.”

sentences.zh: 太皇太后、皇太后崩，司空以特牲告謚於祖廟如儀。

translations.literal: When the grand empress dowager or empress dowager dies, the Minister of Works announces her posthumous title at the ancestral temple with a single victim, as in the observances.
translations.idiomatic: At the death of a grand empress dowager or empress dowager, the Minister of Works reports her temple name to the imperial shrines with a single sacrificial beast, following precedent.

sentences.zh: 長樂太僕、少府、大長秋典喪事，三公奉制度，他皆如禮儀。

translations.literal: The Minister of Transport for Changle, the Privy Treasurer, and the chief eunuch of the palace rear direct the funeral; the three dukes uphold the regulations; all else follows the ritual code.
translations.idiomatic: The Changle Minister of Transport, Privy Treasurer, and chief eunuch superintend obsequies while the three dukes enforce statutory mourning; every other detail mirrors the state liturgy.

sentences.zh: [一] 注[一]丁孚漢儀曰：「永平七年，陰太后崩，晏駕詔曰：『柩將發於殿，腢臣百官陪位，黃門鼓吹三通，鳴鐘鼓，天子舉哀。

translations.literal: [1] Comment [1] Ding Fu’s *Han yi* says: "In Yongping 7 Empress Dowager Yin died; the final edict read: ‘When the catafalque is about to leave the hall, all ministers take station; Yellow Gate musicians sound three calls, bells and drums ring, and the Son of Heaven raises the cry of grief.
translations.idiomatic: [1] Note [1] — Ding Fu’s *Han Ceremonial*: “In Yongping 7 the Yin empress dowager died; her testament ordered: ‘As the bier leaves the hall, the full bureaucracy stands by while Yellow Gate ensembles give three flourishes and bells and drums toll; the emperor leads the lament.’

sentences.zh: 女侍史官三百人皆著素，參以白素，引棺挽歌，下殿就車，黃門宦者引以出宮省。

translations.literal: Three hundred female clerks wear plain white, mixed with white silk, draw the catafalque with dirges, descend the steps to the chariot, and eunuchs of the Yellow Gate lead them from the palace precincts.
translations.idiomatic: Three hundred female scribes in undyed hemp, interwoven with white silk, tow the hearse while singing elegies, carry the stairs to the wagons, and palace eunuchs escort the cortège beyond the inner wards.

sentences.zh: 太后魂車，鸞路，青羽蓋，駟馬，龍旗九旒，前有方相，鳳皇車，大將軍妻參乘，太僕妻御，*[女騎夾轂]*悉道。

translations.literal: The empress dowager’s soul carriage has *luan* fittings, an azure-feather canopy, four-horse team, dragon banner with nine streamers, a *fangxiang* hearse ahead, a phoenix coach, the Grand General’s wife as *cheng* companion, the Minister of Transport’s wife as charioteer, *[female riders flanking the hubs]* all along the route.
translations.idiomatic: Her spirit car uses *luan* regalia, blue-plume awning, four-in-hand, nine-tasseled dragon pennant, exorcist chariot in the van, phoenix coach behind, the Grand General’s consort riding *cheng*, the Minister of Transport’s spouse driving, with squadrons of mounted women flanking the wheel hubs down the avenue.

sentences.zh: 公卿百官如天子郊鹵簿儀。

translations.literal: Dukes, ministers, and the hundred officials follow the suburban escort formation of the Son of Heaven.
translations.idiomatic: Grandees and the bureaucracy array themselves like the sovereign’s suburban procession.

sentences.zh: 』後和熹鄧後葬，案以為儀，自此皆降損於前事也。」

translations.literal: " Later, when Empress Dowager Deng the Harmonious and Brilliant was buried, precedent was taken from this, and thereafter everything was reduced from earlier practice."
translations.idiomatic: “When Empress Deng the Xihe was entombed, this model was codified, and later obsequies were progressively scaled back.”

sentences.zh: 合葬：羨道開通，皇帝謁便房，太常導至羨道，去杖，中常侍受，至柩前，謁，伏哭止如儀。

translations.literal: Joint burial: when the vaulted passage is opened, the emperor visits the side chamber; the Minister of Ceremonies guides him to the gallery, where he lays aside his staff—the chief eunuch receives it—until before the bier he pays respects, prostrates, weeps, and stops as prescribed.
translations.idiomatic: For a consort’s co-inhumation, once the ramp is cleared the sovereign enters the tomb antechamber; the Minister of Ceremonies conducts him to the passage, where he surrenders his cane to a chief eunuch, then approaches the coffin to bow, kowtow, lament, and cease on cue.

sentences.zh: 辭，太常導出，中常侍授杖，升車歸宮。

translations.literal: Taking leave, the Minister of Ceremonies leads him out; the chief eunuch returns the staff; he mounts the carriage and returns to the palace.
translations.idiomatic: When he withdraws, the Minister of Ceremonies escorts him forth, the eunuch hands back the staff, and he rides to the palace.

sentences.zh: 已下，反虞立主如禮。

translations.literal: Thereafter downward, the *yu* rite and tablet installation proceed as in the observances.
translations.idiomatic: From that point the *yu* service and spirit tablet follow ordinary canon.

sentences.zh: 諸郊廟祭服皆下便房。

translations.literal: All suburban and temple sacrificial robes are lowered to the side chamber.
translations.idiomatic: Vestments used at suburban and ancestral rites are deposited in the tomb antechamber.

sentences.zh: 五時朝服各一襲在陵寢，其餘及宴服皆封以篋笥，藏宮殿後合室。

translations.literal: One full set of each season’s court dress remains in the mausoleum dormitory; the rest, including banquet robes, are boxed in wicker hampers and stored in the rear sealed chamber of the palace.
translations.idiomatic: A complete seasonal wardrobe stays in the tomb hall; other garments and festive silks are packed in baskets and sealed in the palace’s rear vault.

sentences.zh: 諸侯王、列侯、始封貴人、公主薨，皆令贈印璽、玉柙銀縷；

translations.literal: When feudatory kings, full marquises, first-enfeoffed exalted ladies, or princesses die, edicts grant them seals, jade shrouds with silver thread,
translations.idiomatic: Feudal kings, full marquises, newly enfeoffed exalted ladies, and princesses receive posthumous seals, jade burial suits laced with silver,

sentences.zh: 大貴人、長公主銅縷。

translations.literal: exalted great ladies and senior princesses receive copper thread.
translations.idiomatic: while senior exalted ladies and chief princesses are granted copper-laced suits.

sentences.zh: 諸侯王、貴人、公主、公、將軍、特進皆賜器，官中二十四物。

translations.literal: Feudatory kings, exalted ladies, princesses, dukes, generals, and specially advanced nobles are all given the twenty-four-piece tomb outfit.
translations.idiomatic: Kings, exalted ladies, princesses, dukes, generals, and nobles of special advancement receive the canonical twenty-four-piece grave set.

sentences.zh: 使者治喪，穿作，柏幟，百官會送，如故事。

translations.literal: Envoys supervise mourning, excavation, cypress banners, and the hundred officials’ joint send-off, according to precedent.
translations.idiomatic: Imperial envoys oversee the wake, shaft-digging, funeral flags, and the bureaucracy’s mass cortège as standing rule prescribes.

sentences.zh: 諸侯王、公主、貴人皆樟棺，洞朱，雲氣畫。

translations.literal: Feudatory kings, princesses, and exalted ladies all receive camphor outer coffins, lacquered cinnabar inside, painted with cloud designs.
translations.idiomatic: Kings, princesses, and exalted ladies are laid in camphor shells, vermilion lacquer within, cloud motifs without.

sentences.zh: 公、特進樟棺黑漆。

translations.literal: Dukes and specially advanced nobles receive camphor coffins in black lacquer.
translations.idiomatic: Dukes and specially advanced peers get camphor coffins finished in black lacquer.

sentences.zh: 中二千石以下坎侯漆。

translations.literal: From attendant two thousand *shi* downward, *kanhou* lacquer is used.
translations.idiomatic: Officials at attendant two thousand *shi* and below receive *kanhou*-style lacquer only.

sentences.zh: [一]朝臣中二千石、將軍，使者弔祭，郡國二千石、六百石以至黃綬，皆賜常車驛牛贈祭。

translations.literal: [1] Court ministers at attendant two thousand *shi* and generals are visited by envoys for condolence sacrifices; commandery and kingdom officers from two thousand *shi* down to holders of the yellow ribbon are all granted regular carts, relay oxen, and mortuary offerings.
translations.idiomatic: [1] Palace ministers at attendant two thousand *shi* and generals receive imperial messengers for lament offerings; local officers from two thousand *shi* to yellow-ribbon rank get standard wagons, post-station oxen, and funeral gifts.

sentences.zh: 宜自佐史以上達，大斂皆以朝服。

translations.literal: From assistants and clerks upward, all wear court dress for the great laying-in.
translations.idiomatic: From assistant rank upward everyone dons court robes for the great enshrouding.

sentences.zh: 君臨吊若遣使者，主人免絰去杖望馬首如禮。

translations.literal: If the ruler attends in person or sends envoys, the host removes head-cord and staff and faces the horses’ heads as ritual requires.
translations.idiomatic: Should the sovereign appear in person or dispatch envoys, the chief mourner strips cord and cane and bows toward the equipage as etiquette demands.

sentences.zh: 免絰去杖，不敢以戚凶服當尊者。

translations.literal: They remove head-cord and staff, not daring to confront exalted persons in harsh mourning dress.
translations.idiomatic: The chief mourner strips cord and cane so as not to present a spectacle of violent grief before superiors.

sentences.zh: [二]自王、主、貴人以下至佐史，送車騎導從吏卒，各如其官府。

translations.literal: [2] From kings, princess-hosts, exalted ladies downward to assistants, escort chariots, cavalry, guides, followers, clerks, and soldiers each match their official rank.
translations.idiomatic: [2] Escort trains—riders, outriders, runners—scale from feudatory sovereigns and princesses down to petty clerks, every detail mirroring the deceased’s bureau.

sentences.zh: 載飾以蓋，龍首魚尾，華布牆，纁上周，交絡前後，雲氣畫帷裳。

translations.literal: The hearse fittings use a canopy, dragon head and fish tail, figured cloth for the “wall,” crimson silk round the upper edge, crossed cords fore and aft, and cloud-painted curtains and valances.
translations.idiomatic: The bier wagon is draped with a dragon-fish crest, brocaded side-screens, a band of scarlet along the roofline, interlaced ropes, and painted cloud hangings.

sentences.zh: 中二千石以上有輜，左龍右虎，朱鳥玄武；

translations.literal: From attendant two thousand *shi* upward there are covered wagons: azure dragon left, white tiger right, vermilion bird, dark warrior.
translations.idiomatic: Officials at attendant two thousand *shi* and above merit the four-emblem hearse—dragon, tiger, sparrow, and tortoise-snake—on the lacquered panels.

sentences.zh: 公侯以上加倚鹿伏熊。

translations.literal: Dukes and marquises upward add reclining deer and crouching bear [figures].
translations.idiomatic: Above ducal rank the screens gain extra zoological bosses—deer couchant and bear prone.

sentences.zh: 千石以下，緇布蓋牆，魚龍首尾而已。

translations.literal: Below one thousand *shi*, black cloth canopy and screen, fish-and-dragon head and tail only.
translations.idiomatic: Lesser ranks make do with black hemp screens and simplified fish-dragon cresting.

sentences.zh: 二百石黃綬以下至於處士，皆以簟席為牆蓋。

translations.literal: From two hundred *shi* yellow ribbon down to recluses, all use bamboo matting for screen and canopy.
translations.idiomatic: From two-hundred-*shi* yellow-ribbon holders to private scholars, bamboo blinds replace silk walls.

sentences.zh: 其正妃、夫人、妻皆如之。

translations.literal: Their principal consorts, ladies, and wives follow the same rule.
translations.idiomatic: Chief consorts, titled ladies, and wives observe the same gradations.

sentences.zh: 諸侯王，傅、相、中尉、內史典喪事，大鴻臚奏謚，天子使者贈璧帛，載日命謚如禮。

translations.literal: For feudatory kings the tutor, chancellor, commandant of attendants, and interior secretary superintend the funeral; the Grand Herald of Guests presents the posthumous title; envoys of the Son of Heaven present jade disks and silk; the day is recorded and the title assigned according to the rites.
translations.idiomatic: Feudal kings rely on tutor, chancellor, commandant, and interior secretary to run obsequies; the Grand Herald forwards the temple name; imperial messengers deliver *bi* disks and bolts of silk; the court fixes the day and bestows the *shi* epithet by statute.

sentences.zh: 下陵，腢臣醳麤服如儀，主人如禮。

translations.literal: After descending the tumulus, all ministers lay aside coarse mourning as in the observances; the hosts likewise act according to the rites.
translations.idiomatic: Once the cortège leaves the mound, the assembly doffs sackcloth on schedule, and the chief mourners mirror each gesture of the code.

sentences.zh: 注[一]丁孚漢儀曰：「孝靈帝葬馬貴人，贈步搖、赤紱葬，青羽蓋、駟馬。

translations.literal: Comment [1] Ding Fu’s *Han yi* says: "When Emperor Ling buried Honored Lady Ma, he granted her a buyao hairpin, a crimson-ribbon burial, an azure-feather canopy, and a four-horse team.
translations.idiomatic: Note [1] — Ding Fu records Lingdi’s obsequies for Lady Ma: step-shaking hairpins, crimson funerary ribbons, peacock-feather awning, team of four.

sentences.zh: 柩下殿，女侍史二百人著素衣輓歌，引木下就車，黃門宦者引出宮門。」

translations.literal: When the catafalque left the hall, two hundred female clerks in plain white sang dirges while lowering the bier onto the wagons; Yellow Gate eunuchs led them out the palace gate."
translations.idiomatic: Two hundred female scribes in undyed hemp towed the coffin with elegies, eased it onto carts, and palace eunuchs escorted the train beyond the inner gate.”

sentences.zh: 贊曰：大禮雖簡，鴻儀則容。

translations.literal: The encomium says: "Though the great rites are concise, the grand observance still has its proper demeanor.
translations.idiomatic: The historian’s *zan* reads: “Even when ritual is spare, the state funeral keeps its stateliness.”

sentences.zh: 天尊地卑，君莊臣恭。

translations.literal: Heaven is honored, earth is lowly; the lord is grave, ministers reverent.
translations.idiomatic: Heaven ranks high, earth low; the ruler stands in awe, servants bow low.

sentences.zh: 質文通變，哀敬交從。

translations.literal: Substance and ornament turn in cycles; grief and awe succeed one another.
translations.idiomatic: Simplicity and splendor alternate across dynasties; sorrow and reverence answer each other in turn.

sentences.zh: 元序斯立，家邦乃隆。

translations.literal: When the primal order is fixed, family and altars flourish.
translations.idiomatic: Once the founding pattern is set, house and realm rise together.
